records.item_title: Body Surface Area (BSA) — Rule of Nines
records.quote: The Wallace Rule of Nines is the quick bedside method for estimating the percent of total body surface area (%TBSA) burned in an adult , and everything on the body is divided into multiples of 9% (plus 1% for the perineum) so the whole body adds to 100% .
records.cite: Lssn 2 — Burn & Inhalation Injury, slides 4, 10, 11, 15, 18

records.item_title: Body Surface Area (BSA) — Rule of Nines
records.quote: A major burn is defined as >20% TBSA .
records.cite: Lssn 2 — Burn & Inhalation Injury, slides 4, 10, 11, 15, 18

records.item_title: Body Surface Area (BSA) — Rule of Nines
records.quote: The single most important reason to get %TBSA right is fluid: %TBSA + patient weight determines the initial fluid resuscitation requirement , and the deck's example resuscitation rate is 4 mL/kg/%TBSA for adults, with half given in the first 8 hours post-burn .
records.cite: Lssn 2 — Burn & Inhalation Injury, slides 4, 10, 11, 15, 18

records.item_title: Body Surface Area (BSA) — Rule of Nines
records.quote: The deck also gives the shortcut that the patient's palm (including fingers) ≈ 1% TBSA for estimating small or scattered burns.
records.cite: Lssn 2 — Burn & Inhalation Injury, slides 4, 10, 11, 15, 18

records.item_title: Body Surface Area (BSA) — Rule of Nines
records.quote: Worked example from the deck: entire anterior trunk + entire right arm = 18% + 9% = 27% TBSA .
records.cite: Lssn 2 — Burn & Inhalation Injury, slides 4, 10, 11, 15, 18

records.quote: Body region (adult) % TBSA Head & neck 9% Each arm (right, left) 9% each Anterior trunk 18% Posterior trunk 18% Each leg (right, left) 18% each Perineum / genital area 1% Total 100% Patient's palm (incl. fingers) — quick estimate ≈1%

records.item_title: Degrees of Burns
records.quote: First degree = epidermis only (red, dry, painful, no blisters ; think sunburn), heals in about 7 days .
records.cite: Lssn 2 — Burn & Inhalation Injury, slides 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 16, 17

records.item_title: Degrees of Burns
records.quote: Second degree = epidermis + part of the dermis (partial-thickness) and splits into superficial partial-thickness (epidermis + superficial dermis, blisters, very painful , heals 10–21 days with no scar ) and deep partial-thickness (epidermis + deep dermis, sweat glands and hair follicles; more nerve endings destroyed so sensation is decreased/variable ; heals 3–8 weeks with permanent scar ).
records.cite: Lssn 2 — Burn & Inhalation Injury, slides 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 16, 17

records.item_title: Degrees of Burns
records.quote: Degree Layers involved Appearance / pain Example Healing First degree (superficial) Epidermis only Red, dry, no blisters , painful Sunburn 7 days Superficial 2nd degree (superficial partial-thickness) Epidermis + superficial dermis Blisters, very painful Hot water scald 10–21 days, no scar Deep 2nd degree (deep partial-thickness) Epidermis + deep dermis , sweat glands, hair follicles Blisters, painful but decreased sensation (nerve endings damaged) Hot liquid, steam, grease, flame 3–8 weeks, permanent scar 3rd degree (full-thickness) Entire epidermis and dermis Charred, pale, leathery; no pain Flame Months , severe scarring, skin grafts necessary 4th degree Entire epidermis and dermis plus fat/muscle, tendon, bone Charred, extends into deep structures Flame Months , severe scarring, multiple grafts necessary Related depth/severity concepts the deck stresses: burns are evaluated for extent (%TBSA), depth, and circumferential components ; the three burn injury zones are zone of coagulation (center = DEAD, irreversible protein denaturation) , zone of stasis (middle = MAYBE, decreased perfusion, salvageable — this is what good resuscitation protects) , and zone of hyperemia (outer = RECOVERS spontaneously) .
records.cite: Lssn 2 — Burn & Inhalation Injury, slides 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 16, 17

records.item_title: Other High-Yield Inhalation-Injury and Burn Content
records.quote: Thermal injury > 1500°C is listed as the injury source, and 20–30% of patients develop upper airway obstruction from progressive edema (usually with temperatures >1000°C ).

records.item_title: Other High-Yield Inhalation-Injury and Burn Content
records.quote: Five predictable events in inhalation injury (memorize the list) (1) acute upper airway obstruction (mucosal edema evolving over time), (2) bronchospasm (intense, from aerosolized irritants, common in the first 24–48 hours , worst in young children because of smaller airways — treat with inhaled bronchodilators), (3) small airway obstruction (treat with humidification + aggressive secretion clearance ), (4) pulmonary infection (develops in 30% to 50% ; pneumonia is a significant complication — treat with culture-directed antibiotics, not prophylaxis), and (5) respiratory failure / ARDS .

records.item_title: Other High-Yield Inhalation-Injury and Burn Content
records.quote: Staging of thermal/smoke injury Early (0–24 hr) — presentation is latent/deceptively mild ; increased secretions, bronchospasm, impaired mucociliary transport, mucus retention, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema (worse with excess resuscitation fluid).

records.item_title: Other High-Yield Inhalation-Injury and Burn Content
records.quote: Intermediate (2–5 days) — upper airway improves while deep pulmonary pathology worsens ; tracheobronchial tree becomes necrotic and sloughs at 3–4 days ; plugging, atelectasis, bacterial colonization ( S. aureus , and gram-negative Klebsiella, Enterobacter, E. coli, Pseudomonas ), ARDS.

records.item_title: Other High-Yield Inhalation-Injury and Burn Content
records.quote: Late (>5 days) — secondary burn-wound infection → sepsis and multi-organ failure , pneumonia, pulmonary emboli risk, long-term restrictive and/or obstructive lung disorders.

records.item_title: Other High-Yield Inhalation-Injury and Burn Content
records.quote: Fluid resuscitation / Parkland The deck names Parkland resuscitation and gives the ABLS adult rate of 4 mL/kg/%TBSA, half in the first 8 hours post-burn , with Lactated Ringer's as the preferred crystalloid (less hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis than normal saline).

records.item_title: Other High-Yield Inhalation-Injury and Burn Content
records.quote: Fluid requirements decline abruptly after 18–24 hours with successful resuscitation — continuing aggressive fluid past that point causes excess edema and pulmonary complications.

records.item_title: Other High-Yield Inhalation-Injury and Burn Content
records.quote: Monitor urine output hourly, goal ~0.5 mL/kg/hr .

records.item_title: Other High-Yield Inhalation-Injury and Burn Content
records.quote: Four phases of burn care (1) initial evaluation and fluid resuscitation (day 1–3 / first ~72 hours — the RT's biggest role) , (2) initial wound excision and biologic closure (days 1–7) , (3) definitive wound closure (day 7 to ~week 6) , (4) rehabilitation/reconstruction/reintegration .

records.item_title: Other High-Yield Inhalation-Injury and Burn Content
records.quote: Ventilator management lung-protective, ARDSnet-style — V_T ≈ 6 mL/kg PBW/IBW, plateau ≤ 30 cm H₂O, appropriate PEEP (balanced against hemodynamics, since high PEEP reduces venous return in a hypovolemic patient), titrate FiO₂ to PaO₂ 55–80 mmHg or SpO₂ 88–95% , avoid prolonged 100% O₂, and allow permissive hypercapnia as long as pH ≥ 7.25 .

records.item_title: What Pulmonary Rehab Is, Its Goals, and Who Qualifies
records.quote: Complete history and physical exam Laboratory testing — CBC, chem profile, α1-antitrypsin titer ECG, ABG analysis, a full PFT battery, and chest x-ray Either a simple exercise-tolerance test ( 6MWT ) or a comprehensive exercise-capacity evaluation Objective criteria from a comprehensive exercise test that justify enrollment: a VO₂max less than 75% of predicted AND a breathing reserve of less than 30%.
records.cite: Heuer Ch 17 — Pulmonary Rehabilitation, Patient Selection, Program Components (PDF p788–790) and Ch 17 T4 Tips (PDF p810) · Heuer Ch 4 — Cardiopulmonary Stress Testing (PDF p221)

records.item_title: Adequate Arterial Oxygenation Limits During Exercise
records.quote: 2 Adequate Arterial Oxygenation Limits During Exercise The floor is SpO₂ 88% / PaO₂ 55 torr.

records.item_title: Adequate Arterial Oxygenation Limits During Exercise
records.quote: Finding at peak activity level Action SpO₂ ≥ 88% ( PaO₂ ≥ 55 torr ) Patient does not need additional O₂ — terminate the test SpO₂ drops ≥ 2% , or SpO₂ < 88% ( PaO₂ < 55 torr ) Increase O₂ by 1 L/min until SpO₂ ≥ 88% AARC safety margin The AARC recommends setting the target SpO₂ during titration to 93% for an extra margin of safety STOP the titration entirely If the SaO₂ drops below 85% Do not start the test If the patient's resting SpO₂ is less than 85% on room air The resulting liter flow is what the ordering physician prescribes for the patient to use during those activities.

records.item_title: Adequate Arterial Oxygenation Limits During Exercise

records.item_title: Inspiratory Muscle Training (IMT)
records.quote: Parameter Recommendation Mode / device Threshold or flow resistor — calibrated threshold preferred Intensity (load) Minimum of 30% of PImax ( lower initial intensity may be needed in COPD patients ); increase by 5% of PImax per week as tolerated Sessions per day 1–2 sessions per day , depending on exercise tolerance Length of sessions Total of 30 minutes per day , divided over 1–2 sessions; initial sessions may need to be limited to 3–5 minutes Days per week 4–6 days per week according to patient tolerance Weeks of training Continue indefinitely to maintain the benefit; functional improvement usually requires at least 5 weeks of training ⚠ The catch patients progressively lose any health-related benefit if they cease training.

records.item_title: Urinary Output (UOP) — Normals, Oliguria, Anuria

records.item_title: Diuretics — Class, Site of Action, and the Electrolyte Problem Each Causes
records.quote: Normal Na⁺ reabsorption is 70% proximal tubule, 20% Loop of Henle, 10% distal tubule ; aldosterone (a mineralocorticoid) increases Na⁺ and H₂O reabsorption in the distal tubule while dumping K⁺ .

records.item_title: Diuretics — Class, Site of Action, and the Electrolyte Problem Each Causes
records.quote: Class Key drug(s) Site of action on the nephron Mechanism / effect Electrolyte & acid-base problems, clinical use Osmotic Mannitol (Aridol); also glycerin, isosorbide, urea Proximal tubule + ascending Loop of Henle Not reabsorbed — pulls water osmotically into the tubule (does NOT primarily block Na⁺); ↑ H₂O and NaCl excretion Cerebral edema / ↑ ICP, TBI ("a brain drug, not a lung drug"); net K⁺ loss ; can transiently worsen pulmonary edema/CHF by first pulling fluid into the bloodstream Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (CAIs) Acetazolamide ; methazolamide, dichlorphenamide Proximal tubule Blocks HCO₃⁻ transport → HCO₃⁻ stays in the urine, Na⁺ follows, water follows → alkaline urine ; very weak diuretic METABOLIC ACIDOSIS (this is the intended effect); used for metabolic alkalosis, altitude sickness, glaucoma ; causes hypokalemia Loop ("high-ceiling") ⭐ Furosemide (Lasix) ; bumetanide, torsemide, ethacrynic acid Ascending Loop of Henle Blocks Na⁺/K⁺/Cl⁻ reabsorption → up to 20% of NaCl and H₂O excreted = most potent #1 for pulmonary edema/CHF ;

records.item_title: Diuretics — Class, Site of Action, and the Electrolyte Problem Each Causes
records.quote: IV vasodilation within 5 minutes (↓ PCWP, BP, SVR) before any diuresis, so WOB and oxygenation improve before urine appears; hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypovolemia, ototoxicity (usually reversible); loses Ca²⁺ Thiazide ⭐ Thiazides Distal tubule Blocks NaCl reabsorption; moderate strength; also ↓ peripheral vascular resistance First-line for mild hypertension ; keeps calcium (opposite of loops); hypokalemia ; ↑ blood glucose / reported DKA (strongest diabetogenic activity); narrow therapeutic margin; not for acute pulmonary edema Potassium-sparing (aldosterone antagonists) ⭐ Spironolactone (Aldactone) , eplerenone (Inspra) Distal convoluted tubule Competitively blocks aldosterone → interferes with Na⁺/K⁺ exchange → lose Na⁺, keep K⁺ Cirrhosis/ascites , hyperaldosteronism; added to loops to protect K⁺;

records.item_title: PEEP — Everything About It
records.quote: Indications intrapulmonary shunting and refractory hypoxemia (consider PEEP when PaO₂/FiO₂ < 200 mmHg ), decreased FRC and decreased lung compliance (reduced compliance greatly increases alveolar opening pressure), and auto-PEEP not responding to ventilator setting adjustments.
records.cite: RCP 105 Lctr 4 — Operating Modes (Chang Ch 4), slides 9, 10, 11, 31; RCP 105 — Management of Mechanical Ventilation (Chang Ch 12), slides 11, 15, 16, 17, 18; RCP 105 Lctr 3 — Principles of MV (Chang/Hess), slides 31, 35, 36, 37, 38, 41, 44, 45, 78 ⚠ "Physiologic PEEP" — STILL ABSENT VAULT-WIDE. The term "physiologic PEEP" (and the variants physiological PEEP , normal PEEP ) does not appear anywhere in the 62 deck files . The vault discusses applied/therapeutic PEEP , auto-PEEP/intrinsic PEEP , and PEEP thresholds ( < 10 cm H₂O as the older Chang ceiling; 10–15 cm H₂O or higher as individualized modern ARDS practice), but never defines a baseline physiologic PEEP value, and never connects glottic closure to an intrinsic end-expiratory pressure. What to look up: the conventional definition of physiologic PEEP as the ~3–5 cm H₂O of end-expiratory pressure normally maintained by the glottis in a non-intubated person (which is lost once the glottis is bypassed by an artificial airway) — check Egan's or the Chang PEEP chapter and confirm the exact number before using it, since no deck in this vault supports any specific value.

records.item_title: Auto-PEEP (Intrinsic / Inadvertent / Occult PEEP)
records.quote: Air trapping / significant airway obstruction (COPD, asthma, secretions) and any patient with a history of air trapping High frequency (> 20/min) , including excessive pressure support ventilation driving the rate up Insufficient inspiratory flow rate → long I-time Insufficient expiratory time — an I:E ratio that is roughly 1:1 or inverse Breath stacking in IMV (a mandatory breath landing on an unfinished spontaneous exhalation) Excessive VT or rate ; tracheal gas insufflation with continuous flow is also listed as a cause How you detect it the high PEEP alarm (triggered when actual PEEP exceeds the preset PEEP limit), rising PIP , and hypotension .
records.cite: RCP 105 — Management of Mechanical Ventilation (Chang Ch 12), slides 32, 33, 34, 35, 70; RCP 105 Lctr 3 — Principles of MV (Chang/Hess), slide 34; RCP 105 Lctr 4 — Operating Modes (Chang Ch 4), slides 9, 18

records.item_title: Auto-PEEP (Intrinsic / Inadvertent / Occult PEEP)
records.quote: How you fix it — give the lungs more time to empty: ↑ flow rate (shortens I-time, lengthens E-time) ↓ VT (shortens I-time) ↓ frequency (f) (lengthens E-time) Keep PS frequency < 20/min ↓ air trapping with bronchodilators in reversible obstruction If setting changes can't correct it, apply therapeutic PEEP to offset the effects of auto-PEEP from small-airway air trapping — therapeutic PEEP is used after you've made the ventilator adjustments, not instead of them.
records.cite: RCP 105 — Management of Mechanical Ventilation (Chang Ch 12), slides 32, 33, 34, 35, 70; RCP 105 Lctr 3 — Principles of MV (Chang/Hess), slide 34; RCP 105 Lctr 4 — Operating Modes (Chang Ch 4), slides 9, 18

records.item_title: High and Low Pressure Alarms and Their Causes
records.quote: They fall into three groups: input power alarms (loss of electricity/battery, loss of air or O₂ pneumatic source < 50 psig ), control circuit alarms (settings out of range, failed Short Self Test [SST] → ventilator inoperative), and output alarms (pressure, volume, flow, time, inspired gas, exhaled gas).

records.item_title: High and Low Pressure Alarms and Their Causes
records.quote: (This is one of the two most important alarms in the control mode, along with low exhaled volume, because the patient is 100% ventilator-dependent.) Low exhaled volume Disconnection, circuit leak, cuff leak; in pressure modes, a fall in compliance or rise in Raw dropping delivered VT; patient effort loss High PEEP Auto-PEEP ; air trapping ; insufficient inspiratory flow (long I-time) ; insufficient expiratory time ; extreme high compliance Low PEEP Circuit leak or ET tube cuff leak (the circuit can't hold the set PEEP) High frequency Patient's need to increase minute ventilation (rapid shallow breathing); incorrect ventilator settings (insufficient flow or insufficient pressure support); excessive sensitivity setting → auto-triggering. ⚠ The high-frequency alarm limit must not be raised without clear justification.

records.item_title: High and Low Pressure Alarms and Their Causes
records.quote: High PIP + normal PPlat = an airway resistance problem (bronchospasm, secretions, ETT obstruction); high PIP + high PPlat = a compliance problem (e.g., ARDS — a patient with V_T 500 mL and PIP 20 cmH₂O who develops ARDS may show the same 500 mL V_T at PIP 35 cmH₂O ).

records.item_title: CPAP (One Pressure) vs. BiPAP (Two Pressures)
records.quote: One more high-yield CPAP fact: the first-line therapy for acute pulmonary edema is CPAP at 8–12 cmH₂O with 100% oxygen .
records.cite: RCP 105 NIV (13-slide), slides 5, 6, 12

records.item_title: Typical Starting Settings and Full Parameter List
records.quote: IPAP 15, EPAP 5, RR 12, FiO₂ 40%, I-Time, Rise .
records.cite: RCP 105 NIV (13-slide), slides 7, 8; RCP 202 BiPAP Basics, slides 1, 2

records.item_title: Typical Starting Settings and Full Parameter List
records.quote: The tidal volume you are aiming for is based on IBW — female IBW = 45 + 2.3 × (inches over 5 ft) , male IBW = 50 + 2.3 × (inches over 5 ft) , then × 8 mL/kg (deck examples: a 5'6" female = 59 kg × 8 = 472 mL , rounded to ~500 mL ; a 6' male = 78 kg × 8 = 624 mL , rounded to ~600 mL ).
records.cite: RCP 105 NIV (13-slide), slides 7, 8; RCP 202 BiPAP Basics, slides 1, 2

records.item_title: Rise, I-Time, and Ramp
records.quote: Ramp helps the patient adapt by gradually/linearly increasing both inspiratory and expiratory pressures (IPAP and EPAP/CPAP) from subtherapeutic levels up to the user-set pressures over a user-set interval ; it helps reduce patient anxiety , and the time can be set to Off or between 5 and 45 minutes .
records.cite: RCP 105 NiPPV Chang Ch 4/7, slides 5, 6, 7; RCP 202 BiPAP Basics, slide 3

records.item_title: BiPAP Alarms
records.quote: Lo VE: normally set to 4 or 5 L/min.
records.cite: RCP 202 BiPAP Basics, slide 4; RCP 105 NiPPV Chang Ch 4/7, slides 12, 13; RCP 105 NIV (13-slide), slide 8

records.item_title: BiPAP Alarms
records.quote: Low Minute Ventilation — start at 4 and adjust to 10–20% lower than the patient's baseline ; and VT alarms set 150 mL above and 150 mL below the observed or desired VT (based on IBW) .
records.cite: RCP 202 BiPAP Basics, slide 4; RCP 105 NiPPV Chang Ch 4/7, slides 12, 13; RCP 105 NIV (13-slide), slide 8

records.item_title: Monitoring — What Defines Success, and When to Quit
records.quote: The failure criterion is time-bound: for a patient in respiratory failure who continues to deteriorate 30 minutes after the initiation of NIV, the best option is to intubate and initiate mechanical ventilation.
records.cite: RCP 105 NIV (13-slide), slides 4, 12

records.item_title: Normal Blood Gas Values — Memorize This Table
records.quote: Blood Gas Value Arterial Venous pH 7.35 – 7.45 7.30 – 7.40 PaCO₂ 35 – 45 mm Hg 42 – 48 mm Hg HCO₃⁻ 22 – 28 mEq/L (NBRC uses 22 – 26 ) 24 – 30 mEq/L PaO₂ 80 – 100 mm Hg 35 – 45 mm Hg Base Excess (BE) –2 to +2 mEq/L –2 to +2 mEq/L Know why the venous column differs: venous pH is slightly lower because of acid production in the tissues ; venous CO₂ is higher because that blood is carrying CO₂ back from the tissues to the lungs ; venous bicarbonate is slightly higher because of ongoing buffering and metabolic activity in the peripheral tissues ; and venous oxygen is much lower because oxygen has already been delivered to the tissues .
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slide 4

records.item_title: Normal Blood Gas Values — Memorize This Table
records.quote: The single memorized "perfect" gas the deck uses for every calculation is pH 7.40 / PaCO₂ 40 mm Hg / HCO₃⁻ 24 mEq/L .
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slide 4

records.item_title: Normal SaO₂ Value
records.quote: It appears only inside case studies as reported patient data ( SaO₂ 95% in the chronic ventilatory failure case, SaO₂ 97% in the DKA case) and in the note that SaO₂ is a CALCULATED value, not a directly measured one .
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 4, 20, 36, 64

records.item_title: Normal SaO₂ Value
records.quote: Look up the standard normal SaO₂ 95–100% in your RCP 101/103 notes or textbook and confirm the number your instructor wants.
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 4, 20, 36, 64

records.item_title: PaCO₂ — The RESPIRATORY Component
records.quote: 4 PaCO₂ — The RESPIRATORY Component PaCO₂ (normal 35 – 45 mm Hg) is the respiratory component of the ABG and it is controlled by the lungs , which regulate it moment-to-moment .
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 4, 6, 22, 50

records.item_title: HCO₃⁻ — The METABOLIC Component
records.quote: 5 HCO₃⁻ — The METABOLIC Component HCO₃⁻ (normal 22 – 28 mEq/L arterial;
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 4, 18, 22, 43

records.item_title: HCO₃⁻ — The METABOLIC Component
records.quote: Renal compensation is slow — 3 to 5 days minimum .
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 4, 18, 22, 43

records.item_title: PaO₂ — Oxygenation
records.quote: 6 PaO₂ — Oxygenation PaO₂ (normal 80 – 100 mm Hg) reflects the oxygen tension in arterial blood and tells you about oxygenation , not acid-base — but you must always read it alongside the pH and PaCO₂ , because severe hypoxemia can create a MIXED disorder .
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 4, 9, 12, 70

records.item_title: PaO₂ — Oxygenation
records.quote: Two clinical thresholds to know: when PaO₂ drops to about 60 mm Hg , the peripheral chemoreceptors are stimulated and signal the brain to increase ventilation (that is why hypoxemia is the most common cause of acute alveolar hyperventilation ); and when PaO₂ is severely low , tissues switch to anaerobic metabolism and produce lactic acid , adding a metabolic acidosis on top of whatever else is happening, making both the pH and the HCO₃⁻ lower than expected for that PaCO₂.
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 4, 9, 12, 70

records.item_title: PaO₂ — Oxygenation
records.quote: In COPD , a lower PaO₂ (around 55–60 mm Hg) can be acceptable for hypoxic drive.
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 4, 9, 12, 70

records.item_title: Base Excess (BE)
records.quote: 7 Base Excess (BE) Base Excess normally ranges from –2 to +2 mEq/L in both arterial and venous blood.
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 4, 64

records.item_title: Measured vs. Calculated Values — Know the Split
records.quote: Quality control runs control solutions at three levels — acidotic, alkalotic, and normal — in ampules of 2–3 mL , and results must fall within ±2 standard deviations ; anything outside that range is an error .
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 64, 65, 66, 67

records.item_title: Systematic ABG Interpretation Steps
records.quote: 13 Systematic ABG Interpretation Steps 1 · clinical assessment 2 · pH 7.35 – 7.45 3 · PaCO₂ 35 – 45 mm Hg 4 · HCO₃⁻ 22 – 26 mmol/L 5 · compare all three name the disorder 6 · compensation un / partial / full 7 · oxygenation separately, last acid–base first · oxygenation second — never interleaved a normal pH does not mean normal physiology — step 6 exists because of compensation Steps 2–4 gather three numbers; step 5 is where they are compared against each other to name the disorder.
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 2, 69

records.item_title: Systematic ABG Interpretation Steps
records.quote: The deck's example: an ABG showing acute respiratory acidosis in a patient who is alert, in no distress, and saturating 98% should be questioned — suspect sampling error, processing delay, or wrong patient .
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 2, 69

records.item_title: Acid-Base Disorder Patterns — The Master Table
records.quote: Disorder pH PaCO₂ HCO₃⁻ PaO₂ Deck's Example Acute alveolar hyperventilation w/ hypoxemia (acute respiratory alkalosis , uncompensated) ↑ > 7.45 ↓ < 35 decreased but still normal decreased pH 7.52 / PaCO₂ 28 / HCO₃⁻ 22 / PaO₂ 61 Acute ventilatory failure w/ hypoxemia (acute respiratory acidosis , uncompensated) ↓ < 7.35 ↑ > 45 increased but still normal decreased pH 7.16 / PaCO₂ 79 / HCO₃⁻ 26 / PaO₂ 57 Chronic ventilatory failure w/ hypoxemia ( COMPENSATED respiratory acidosis) NORMAL increased increased significantly decreased pH 7.36 / PaCO₂ 79 / HCO₃⁻ 43 / PaO₂ 61 Acute alveolar hyperventilation ON chronic ventilatory failure ↑ (alkalosis) ↓ from the chronic baseline ↑ (chronic compensation) decreased pH 7.52 / PaCO₂ 51 / HCO₃⁻ 40 / PaO₂ 46 Acute ventilatory failure ON chronic ventilatory failure ↓ (acidosis) ↑↑ from the chronic baseline ↑ (chronic compensation) decreased pH 7.28 / PaCO₂ 99 / HCO₃⁻ 45 / PaO₂ 34 Metabolic alkalosis increased normal increased normal pH 7.56 / PaCO₂ 44 / HCO₃⁻ 27 / PaO₂ 94 Metabolic acidosis decreased normal decreased normal pH 7.26 / PaCO₂ 37 / HCO₃⁻ 18 / PaO₂ 94 Lactic acidosis (metabolic acidosis w/ hypoxemia) decreased normal or decreased decreased DECREASED pH 7.21 / PaCO₂ 35 / HCO₃⁻ 14 / PaO₂ 34 The side-by-side comparison slide is worth memorizing on its own — from a chronic ventilatory failure baseline of pH 7.36 / PaCO₂ 77 / HCO₃⁻ 43 / PaO₂ 61 , an acute ventilatory failure on top drives it to 7.28 / 99 / 44 / 39 , while an acute hyperventilation on top drives it to 7.51 / 52 / 40 / 49 .
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 10, 11, 16, 18, 24, 25, 26, 30, 33, 34

records.item_title: Compensation — Uncompensated, Partially Compensated, Fully Compensated
records.quote: 15 Compensation — Uncompensated, Partially Compensated, Fully Compensated UNCOMPENSATED means the opposite system has not had time to respond yet — this is what every ACUTE pattern in the table above shows: in acute ventilatory failure the HCO₃⁻ is "increased but remains within the normal range because there has been little to no renal compensation yet." PARTIALLY COMPENSATED means the opposite system is adjusting but the pH is STILL abnormal — the deck's DKA case is the textbook example: pH 6.98 with PaCO₂ driven down to 24 mm Hg by Kussmaul respirations — the compensation helps but cannot normalize the pH because the metabolic derangement is extreme .
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 16, 18, 20, 22, 32, 36, 69

records.item_title: Compensation — Uncompensated, Partially Compensated, Fully Compensated
records.quote: Timing is the tell: the LUNGS compensate fast (moment-to-moment); the KIDNEYS take 3 to 5 days.
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 16, 18, 20, 22, 32, 36, 69

records.item_title: Quick Calculations — ACUTE PaCO₂ Changes
records.quote: For every 10 mm Hg INCREASE in PaCO₂ : pH falls ~0.06 units and HCO₃⁻ rises ~1 mEq/L (from buffering, before any renal compensation).
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 6, 7, 8, 9

records.item_title: Quick Calculations — ACUTE PaCO₂ Changes
records.quote: For every 20 mm Hg increase : pH falls ~0.12 and HCO₃⁻ rises ~2 mEq/L .
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 6, 7, 8, 9

records.item_title: Quick Calculations — ACUTE PaCO₂ Changes
records.quote: PaCO₂ rises from 40 to 60 (a 20 mm Hg change) → 20 ÷ 10 = 2 → 2 × 0.06 = 0.12 → expected pH 7.40 − 0.12 = 7.28 , and HCO₃⁻ = 24 + (2 × 1) = 26 mEq/L .
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 6, 7, 8, 9

records.item_title: Quick Calculations — CHRONIC PaCO₂ Changes and Renal Compensation
records.quote: 17 Quick Calculations — CHRONIC PaCO₂ Changes and Renal Compensation Chronic changes occur when the ventilatory problem persists for several days , and the kidneys respond by adjusting HCO₃⁻ — a process that takes 3 to 5 days minimum .
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slide 22

records.item_title: Quick Calculations — CHRONIC PaCO₂ Changes and Renal Compensation
records.quote: From the same pH 7.40 / PaCO₂ 40 / HCO₃⁻ 24 baseline: for every 10 mm Hg INCREASE in PaCO₂ , HCO₃⁻ rises by ~3.5 – 4 mEq/L ; for every 10 mm Hg DECREASE in PaCO₂ , HCO₃⁻ falls by ~4 – 5 mEq/L .
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slide 22

records.item_title: Quick Calculations — CHRONIC PaCO₂ Changes and Renal Compensation
records.quote: Compare those numbers to the acute rule ( ~1 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg ) and you can see the whole point — a big bicarbonate move means CHRONIC, a small one means ACUTE.
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slide 22

records.item_title: Quick Calculations — Metabolic Compensation Rules
records.quote: METABOLIC ALKALOSIS: for every 1 mEq/L INCREASE in HCO₃⁻, PaCO₂ should INCREASE by 0.7 mm Hg.
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 29, 33, 36

records.item_title: Quick Calculations — Metabolic Compensation Rules
records.quote: HCO₃⁻ goes 24 → 29 (a rise of 5), so the expected PaCO₂ rise = 0.7 × 5 = 3.5 mm Hg.
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 29, 33, 36

records.item_title: Quick Calculations — Metabolic Compensation Rules
records.quote: METABOLIC ACIDOSIS: for every 1 mEq/L DECREASE in HCO₃⁻, PaCO₂ should DECREASE by 1.2 mm Hg — and note the timing: this respiratory compensation begins within the FIRST HOUR and is complete by 12 to 24 hours (versus 3–5 days for renal compensation).
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 29, 33, 36

records.item_title: Anion Gap
records.quote: The measured players are the cation Na⁺ and the anions Cl⁻ and HCO₃⁻ , with normal plasma values Na⁺ 140 mEq/L, Cl⁻ 105 mEq/L, HCO₃⁻ 24 mEq/L .

records.item_title: Anion Gap
Anion Gap
records.quote: The normal range is 9 to 14 mEq/L .

records.item_title: Anion Gap
records.quote: An anion gap ABOVE 14 mEq/L indicates metabolic acidosis from the ACCUMULATION OF FIXED ACIDS — lactic acids, keto acids, salicylate intoxication — because those acids release H⁺ that consumes HCO₃⁻ while adding unmeasured anions .

records.item_title: Mechanisms That Reduce PaCO₂ (Causes of Acute Alveolar Hyperventilation)
records.quote: 21 Mechanisms That Reduce PaCO₂ (Causes of Acute Alveolar Hyperventilation) Hypoxemia is the MOST COMMON cause — when PaO₂ drops to around 60 mm Hg , the peripheral chemoreceptors sense it and signal the brain to increase the ventilatory rate , more CO₂ is exhaled, and you get respiratory alkalosis (↑ pH, ↓ PaCO₂) .
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 12, 13, 15

records.item_title: Chronic Ventilatory Failure — Why the Patient Chooses CO₂ Retention
records.quote: The result is chronic ventilatory failure with hypoxemia = compensated respiratory acidosis (deck example pH 7.36 / PaCO₂ 79 / HCO₃⁻ 43 / PaO₂ 61 ; the case study patient was alert, comfortable, RR 11 , with pH 7.39 / PaCO₂ 67 / HCO₃⁻ 39 / PaO₂ 76 / SaO₂ 95% ).
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 18, 19, 20, 21

records.item_title: The Trap — Acute Hyperventilation on Chronic Ventilatory Failure
records.quote: He was in impending ventilatory failure ; he fatigued, his RR fell, PaCO₂ climbed above baseline, and he died 17 hours later .
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 23, 24, 25, 26, 27

records.item_title: ABG Sampling — Sites, Allen's Test, and Procedure
records.quote: Perform a modified Allen's test before any radial draw to confirm collateral circulation — the hand should pink up within 1–2 seconds after releasing the ulnar artery; if it does not, use another site .
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 50, 51, 71, 72, 73

records.item_title: ABG Sampling — Sites, Allen's Test, and Procedure
records.quote: Procedure order: check the physician order → gather and assemble supplies → wash hands → introduce yourself → identify the patient with two identifiers and verify O₂ settings → explain the procedure → prepare the syringe (needle secure, BEVEL UP, plunger drawn back) → locate and palpate the artery → modified Allen's test → clean the site → puncture → hold pressure at least 5 minutes or until bleeding stops → engage the safety device → place the filter cap and remove air → label with patient ID, O₂ settings, and time → run the sample within 10–30 minutes or place it on ice → dispose in a sharps container.
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 50, 51, 71, 72, 73

records.item_title: Common Errors That Affect ABG Accuracy
records.quote: PREANALYTIC (before or after analysis — air bubbles, wrong anticoagulant, venous contamination, delays), ANALYTIC (during analysis — malfunctioning electrodes, poor QC), POSTANALYTIC (recording — wrong patient info, transcription mistakes, failing to record FiO₂ , sampling less than 20 minutes after an FiO₂ change ), and INTERPRETATION errors (misclassifying the result, e.g. confusing compensated respiratory acidosis with metabolic acidosis ).
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 53, 54, 55, 74

records.item_title: Common Errors That Affect ABG Accuracy
records.quote: Puncture-site hazards: hematoma (disrupts blood flow), bleeding ( hold pressure ≥ 5 min , longer on anticoagulants ), clotting and vessel spasm , and tissue trauma to muscles, bones, and nerves.
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 53, 54, 55, 74

records.item_title: Arterial Lines and Point-of-Care Testing
records.quote: To sample: withdraw approximately 3–5 mL of fluid to clear the dead space, attach the ABG syringe to the sampling port and collect , return the 3–5 mL to the patient (closed systems — this prevents hospital-acquired anemia; open systems require discarding it ), then flush the catheter — and if the waveform fails to return, the stopcock is in the wrong position and the line needs to be zeroed.
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 56, 57, 58, 62, 63, 68

records.item_title: Arterial Lines and Point-of-Care Testing
records.quote: Point-of-care testing at the bedside — the I-Stat delivers ABG results within 90 seconds and can run other lab tests.
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slides 56, 57, 58, 62, 63, 68

records.item_title: Special Considerations — When the ABG Lies
records.quote: COPD: look for chronic CO₂ retention — high PaCO₂ with renal compensation means the pH may look normal , and a lower PaO₂ (around 55–60 mm Hg) can be acceptable for hypoxic drive.
records.cite: RCP 103 ABG Assessments, slide 70

records.item_title: Epidemiology — how common is asthma?
records.quote: In the United States (CDC/NCHS) , about 25 million people have asthma — 18.4 million adults ( 7.6% ) and 6.2 million children ( 8.4% ).
records.cite: Asthma PP, slide 5

records.item_title: Epidemiology — how common is asthma?
records.quote: Asthma accounts for 6.5% of all physician office visits and roughly 1.9 million emergency department visits per year, and causes 3,651 deaths per year.
records.cite: Asthma PP, slide 5

records.item_title: Epidemiology — how common is asthma?
records.quote: Worldwide ( WHO ), about 235 million people have asthma, more than 80% of asthma deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries , and asthma is the most common chronic disease among children worldwide.
records.cite: Asthma PP, slide 5

records.item_title: Pathophysiology — the immunologic mechanism and the early vs. late phase
records.quote: The early phase starts within minutes and usually resolves within about 1 hour ; the late phase starts hours later as eosinophils, basophils, neutrophils, and T-cells migrate in, and lasts longer.
records.cite: Asthma PP, slides 14-15, 17

records.item_title: Asthma phenotypes
records.quote: BMI > 30 Harder to control
records.cite: Asthma PP, slide 4

records.item_title: How is asthma diagnosed? (Spirometry numbers you must know)
records.quote: Test Diagnostic threshold Spirometry ↓ FEV₁ and ↓ FEV₁/FVC ; adults < 0.75–0.80 , children < 0.90 Bronchodilator response (reversibility) ↑ FEV₁ ≥ 12% and/or ≥ 200 mL ; children ↑ FEV₁ ≥ 12% of predicted Peak expiratory flow (PEFR) variability Daily variability > 10% (adults), > 13% (children) After 4 weeks anti-inflammatory therapy ↑ FEV₁ ≥ 12% or PEFR ↑ ≥ 20% Methacholine challenge (bronchial provocation) ≥ 20% decrease in FEV₁ = airway hyperresponsiveness
records.cite: Asthma PP, slides 6, 19, 23

records.item_title: Physical exam, chest x-ray, ABG, and lab findings
records.quote: In severe episodes, pulsus paradoxus — an exaggerated drop in systolic BP of > 10 mmHg during inspiration from severe air trapping impeding venous return — is a red flag.
records.cite: Asthma PP, slides 20-21, 25-26

records.item_title: Disease severity classification — exacerbation severity (Mild / Moderate / Severe / Imminent arrest)
records.quote: I:E ≈ 1:2 RR often > 30/min , marked retractions Paradoxical thoracoabdominal movement PEFR ≥ 80% predicted or personal best 50–80% predicted or personal best < 50% predicted — SaO₂ > 95% 92–95% < 92% — Pulsus paradoxus — — > 25 mmHg Loss of pulsus paradoxus (muscle fatigue) Other — — — Bradycardia ; rising PaCO₂ ; respiratory acidosis (failure) A silent chest is never improvement — it is a late, critical warning that airflow has nearly stopped.
records.cite: Asthma PP, slides 27-28

records.item_title: Chronic severity classification (Intermittent / Mild, Moderate, Severe Persistent) and Steps 1–6
records.quote: 14 Chronic severity classification (Intermittent / Mild, Moderate, Severe Persistent) and Steps 1–6 INTERMITTENT ≤ 2 days/week MILD persistent > 2 days/wk, not daily MODERATE daily symptoms SEVERE persistent throughout the day Step 1 Step 2 Step 3 or 4 Step 5 or 6 severity = the lowest level of treatment required to maintain control The classification is defined by the treatment needed to hold control — which is why severity and step are two views of the same thing.
records.cite: Asthma PP, slides 6, 33; Ch 12 Nonsteroidal, slides 6-7, 9, 21, 29, 31-34, 36

records.item_title: Chronic severity classification (Intermittent / Mild, Moderate, Severe Persistent) and Steps 1–6
records.quote: What the decks state Deck source Management uses a stepwise approach ; step up (short-term or sustained) for poor control, step down after ≥ 3 months of stable control Asthma PP, slides 6, 33 Step 2 = mild persistent asthma ;
records.cite: Asthma PP, slides 6, 33; Ch 12 Nonsteroidal, slides 6-7, 9, 21, 29, 31-34, 36

records.quote: Category What it does Onset / Duration Generic drugs Brand names Ultra-short-acting β-agonist Rapid bronchodilation; mainly upper-airway mucosal vasoconstriction/edema (croup, post-extubation stridor, epiglottitis), not routine asthma Onset 3–5 min , duration < 3 hr (~ 2 hr ) Racemic epinephrine Generic (SVN 2.25% , 0.25–0.5 mL ) SABA (reliever / rescue) β₂ stimulation → bronchodilation for acute bronchospasm Onset 15 min , peak 30–60 min , duration 4–6 hr Albuterol ;

records.item_title: SABA vs. LABA vs. Controller medications — the master table
records.quote: Xopenex (~5–8 hr) SABA + SAMA β₂ stimulation + acetylcholine blockade; add-on for persistent/severe bronchospasm Duration ~6 hr Ipratropium / Albuterol DuoNeb , Combivent LABA (controller — never alone in asthma) Maintenance bronchodilation, control of bronchospasm, nocturnal protection Onset 20 min , duration 12–24 hr Salmeterol , Formoterol , Arformoterol , Indacaterol , Olodaterol , Vilanterol ; extended-release albuterol Serevent Diskus;

records.item_title: SABA vs. LABA vs. Controller medications — the master table
records.quote: Fluticasone furoate/Vilanterol Advair , Symbicort , Dulera , Breo (Ellipta) Controller — Leukotriene modifiers Oral anti-inflammatory; good for allergic and exercise-induced asthma Daily, oral Montelukast ⭐, Zafirlukast , Zileuton Singulair, Accolate, Zyflo / Zyflo CR Controller — Mast cell stabilizer Blocks mast cell degranulation before inflammation starts Daily, prophylactic Cromolyn (disodium cromoglycate) Generic only (SVN 20 mg/2 mL, 1% ) Controller — Monoclonal antibodies (biologics) Injectable add-on for severe asthma; block IgE or IL-5/eosinophils Injection / infusion Omalizumab (IgE);
records.cite: Asthma PP, slides 31, 36-37; Ch 6 Adrenergics, slides 11, 17-18, 23, 30-31, 34-37, 39-42; Ch 12 Nonsteroidal, slides 4, 8-9, 21, 26-28, 34

records.item_title: SABA details and side effects you get asked about
records.quote: 16 SABA details and side effects you get asked about Albuterol is the most-used SABA — nebulized typically 2.5 mg in 3 mL normal saline, or by MDI; it is a saligenin agent (catechol nucleus modified at the carbon-3 site for β₂ selectivity), available as MDI, DPI, nebulizer, syrup, and extended-release tablets .
records.cite: Ch 6 Adrenergics, slides 23, 26, 28-33, 54, 56-57; Asthma PP, slide 36

records.item_title: SABA details and side effects you get asked about
records.quote: Levalbuterol (Xopenex) is the pure (R)-isomer of albuterol — the R-isomer does the bronchodilating, the S-isomer is roughly 100× less potent and may worsen airway responsiveness; levalbuterol comes in 0.31, 0.63, and 1.25 mg/3 mL plus a 1.25 mg/0.5 mL concentrate.
records.cite: Ch 6 Adrenergics, slides 23, 26, 28-33, 54, 56-57; Asthma PP, slide 36

records.item_title: SABA details and side effects you get asked about
records.quote: Side effects: tremor , tachycardia (watch for a 20 bpm or 20% increase over baseline — the stop-and-notify threshold), palpitations , hypertension or hypotension, headache, nausea/vomiting, hypokalemia , hyperglycemia , a fall in PaO₂ from worsened V/Q matching, tolerance/loss of bronchoprotection, and paradoxical bronchospasm .
records.cite: Ch 6 Adrenergics, slides 23, 26, 28-33, 54, 56-57; Asthma PP, slide 36

records.item_title: SABA details and side effects you get asked about
records.quote: Catecholamines are inactivated by COMT (duration only 1.5–3 hr ) and by heat, light, and air , so they are useless orally.
records.cite: Ch 6 Adrenergics, slides 23, 26, 28-33, 54, 56-57; Asthma PP, slide 36

records.item_title: LABA details and the LABA safety rule
records.quote: Salmeterol (Serevent Diskus) is DPI only, onset 20 min (slower than albuterol), peak at 3–5 hours , duration 12 hours .
records.cite: Ch 6 Adrenergics, slides 17, 34-37, 39-43, 47

records.item_title: LABA details and the LABA safety rule
records.quote: Formoterol is β₂-selective with a fast 3-minute onset and up to 12 hours duration, available as SVN and DPI , approved for asthma maintenance and prevention of exercise-induced bronchospasm in adults and children ≥ 5 years .
records.cite: Ch 6 Adrenergics, slides 17, 34-37, 39-43, 47

records.item_title: LABA details and the LABA safety rule
records.quote: Arformoterol (Brovana) is a single isomer of formoterol, nebulizer solution, 12 hours , approved for COPD maintenance .
records.cite: Ch 6 Adrenergics, slides 17, 34-37, 39-43, 47

records.item_title: LABA details and the LABA safety rule
records.quote: Indacaterol (Arcapta) and Olodaterol (Striverdi Respimat) are ultra-long-acting at up to 24 hours , both COPD maintenance.
records.cite: Ch 6 Adrenergics, slides 17, 34-37, 39-43, 47

records.item_title: Controller medication details — how each class actually works
records.quote: Mast cell stabilizers (Cromolyn) prevent mast cell degranulation before mediators are released — prophylactic use only , never during acute bronchospasm, and it can take 2–4 weeks to show improvement; note GINA does not include Cromolyn as an asthma treatment agent.
records.cite: Asthma PP, slide 37; Ch 12 Nonsteroidal, slides 4, 6, 8-9, 21-22, 26-29, 31-36

records.item_title: Controller medication details — how each class actually works
records.quote: Antileukotrienes split into receptor blockers — Montelukast (Singulair) ⭐ most-tested, oral 4 mg , 10 mg , 5 mg chewable , and Zafirlukast (Accolate) , 10 mg bid ages 5–11 , 20 mg bid ages 12+ — and a synthesis inhibitor , Zileuton (Zyflo) , 600 mg QID , which inhibits the 5-lipoxygenase (5-LO) enzyme and requires liver function monitoring and caution with theophylline and warfarin .
records.cite: Asthma PP, slide 37; Ch 12 Nonsteroidal, slides 4, 6, 8-9, 21-22, 26-29, 31-36

records.item_title: Controller medication details — how each class actually works
records.quote: Antileukotrienes work in only about 50–70% of patients and are not optimal as monotherapy .
records.cite: Asthma PP, slide 37; Ch 12 Nonsteroidal, slides 4, 6, 8-9, 21-22, 26-29, 31-36

records.item_title: Peak flow meters and the asthma action plan zones
records.quote: Zone Peak flow (% of personal best) Clinical status Action Green 80–100% Well controlled — no symptoms, usual activities possible Continue daily controller medications as prescribed Yellow 50–80% Worsening control — increased symptoms, increased SABA use, nighttime awakening Increase rescue medication per plan, continue controller, contact provider if no improvement, aim to return to Green Red < 50% Severe / poor control — severe SOB, symptoms > 24 hours , limited activity Use rescue medication immediately , add systemic therapy if prescribed, contact provider urgently Emergency signs — Life-threatening — difficulty walking or talking from dyspnea, cyanosis of lips or nails, severe distress Call 911 / go to the hospital immediately Peak flow also supports the diagnosis of asthma: daily variability > 10% in adults / > 13% in children, or PEFR improvement ≥ 20% after anti-inflammatory therapy.
records.cite: Asthma PP, slides 23, 33-35; Ch 6 Adrenergics, slide 56; Ch 12 Nonsteroidal, slide 37

records.item_title: Indications for mechanical ventilation / intubation of the asthmatic
records.quote: Before intubation, escalate: oxygen therapy up to CPAP/BiPAP , continuous nebulized albuterol (generally 10–15 mg/hour in an adult, specifically used to try to avoid respiratory failure, intubation, and mechanical ventilation ), and adjuncts such as heliox , magnesium sulfate , and subcutaneous epinephrine .
records.cite: Asthma PP, slides 21, 28, 31; Ch 6 Adrenergics, slide 52

records.item_title: Diagnosis — the FEV1/FVC criterion and GOLD's clinical triggers
records.quote: The diagnosis is confirmed only by spirometry: a post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC < 0.70 .
records.cite: COPD PP, slides 16, 18-19

records.item_title: Diagnosis — the FEV1/FVC criterion and GOLD's clinical triggers
records.quote: In COPD the FEV₁ falls more than the FVC because obstruction slows expiration, which is what drags the ratio down; a normal person exhales about 80–85% of the FVC in the first second, versus roughly 66% in the example COPD spirogram.
records.cite: COPD PP, slides 16, 18-19

records.item_title: GOLD stages — severity of airflow limitation
records.quote: 4 GOLD stages — severity of airflow limitation post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC < 0.70 — required for every grade GOLD 1 · Mild FEV₁ ≥ 80% GOLD 2 · Moderate 50 ≤ FEV₁ < 80% GOLD 3 · Severe 30 ≤ FEV₁ < 50% GOLD 4 · V. severe FEV₁ < 30% the ratio makes the diagnosis · the FEV₁ percent predicted sets the grade FEV₁ and FVC alone correlate poorly with dyspnea, function, survival, and treatment response All four grades share the same diagnostic ratio; only the FEV₁ percent predicted separates them.
records.cite: COPD PP, slide 20

records.item_title: GOLD stages — severity of airflow limitation
records.quote: These stages are applied after obstruction is already confirmed by a post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC < 0.70 .
records.cite: COPD PP, slide 20

records.item_title: GOLD stages — severity of airflow limitation
records.quote: GOLD stage Severity Post-bronchodilator FEV₁ % predicted GOLD 1 Mild ≥ 80% predicted GOLD 2 Moderate 50–79% predicted GOLD 3 Severe 30–49% predicted GOLD 4 Very severe ≤ 30% predicted
records.cite: COPD PP, slide 20

records.item_title: GOLD assessment — symptoms (mMRC and CAT) and the A/B/C/D groups
records.quote: The mMRC (Modified Medical Research Council) dyspnea scale runs 0 to 4 and measures breathlessness only; score < 1 = low risk , score ≥ 2 = high risk , and it predicts mortality.
records.cite: COPD PP, slides 17, 21-26

records.item_title: GOLD assessment — symptoms (mMRC and CAT) and the A/B/C/D groups
records.quote: The CAT (COPD Assessment Test) is an 8-item questionnaire, each item scored 0 to 5 for a total of 0 to 40 , covering cough, mucus, chest tightness, breathlessness with activity, confidence leaving home, sleep, and energy; score < 10 = low risk , score ≥ 10 = high risk .
records.cite: COPD PP, slides 17, 21-26

records.item_title: GOLD assessment — symptoms (mMRC and CAT) and the A/B/C/D groups
records.quote: Group Symptoms CAT FEV₁ % predicted Exacerbations/year Hospitalizations Initial pharmacologic therapy A Fewer symptoms, low risk < 10 50–79% ≤ 1 None A bronchodilator — SABA or LABA ;
records.cite: COPD PP, slides 17, 21-26

records.item_title: GOLD assessment — symptoms (mMRC and CAT) and the A/B/C/D groups
records.quote: SABA as needed for rescue B More symptoms, low risk ≥ 10 50–79% ≤ 1 None LABA or LAMA (e.g., Spiriva);
records.cite: COPD PP, slides 17, 21-26

records.item_title: GOLD assessment — symptoms (mMRC and CAT) and the A/B/C/D groups
records.quote: SABA for rescue C Fewer symptoms, high risk < 10 30–49% ≥ 2 ≥ 1 in last year LAMA (best at reducing exacerbations); often dual LAMA + LABA or LABA + ICS ;
records.cite: COPD PP, slides 17, 21-26

records.item_title: GOLD assessment — symptoms (mMRC and CAT) and the A/B/C/D groups
records.quote: SABA for rescue D More symptoms, high risk ≥ 10 30–49% ≥ 2 ≥ 1 in last year Combination from the start — LAMA + LABA or LABA + ICS ; individualized, may add roflumilast (Daliresp) or azithromycin Roflumilast (Daliresp) is not a steroid — it is a phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE-4) inhibitor that reduces inflammation and exacerbations in severe COPD.
records.cite: COPD PP, slides 17, 21-26

records.item_title: Chronic bronchitis — the "Blue Bloater" (Type B COPD)
records.quote: 8 Chronic bronchitis — the "Blue Bloater" (Type B COPD) Chronic bronchitis is defined clinically : a chronic productive cough for ≥ 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years , after excluding other causes.
records.cite: COPD PP, slides 3-5

records.item_title: Increased risk factors because of COPD (what having COPD puts you at risk for)
records.quote: Exacerbation risk is itself self-reinforcing: the best predictor of a future exacerbation is a prior one , especially ≥ 2 exacerbations in the past year or any exacerbation requiring hospitalization , and that risk rises significantly in GOLD 3 and GOLD 4 patients because their baseline lung function is already severely reduced.
records.cite: COPD PP, slides 3, 27, 29

records.item_title: Alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency — the numbers
records.quote: A serum level below 15% to 20% of the normal value is highly suggestive of emphysema caused by AATD.
records.cite: COPD PP, slides 7, 11

records.item_title: COPD exacerbation — definition and severity
records.quote: The best predictor of a future exacerbation is a history of prior exacerbations — especially ≥ 2 in the past year or any requiring hospitalization.
records.cite: COPD PP, slide 27

records.item_title: LTOT — long-term oxygen therapy qualifying criteria (PaO₂ and SpO₂ thresholds)
records.quote: 19 LTOT — long-term oxygen therapy qualifying criteria (PaO₂ and SpO₂ thresholds) The decision threshold for continuous long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) in COPD is SaO₂ ≤ 88% or PaO₂ ≤ 55 torr on room air — meeting either qualifies the patient for home O₂ .
records.cite: RCP 203 Lesson 3a Ch 4 — Evaluate Procedure Results, slide 66 (LTOT + nocturnal O₂ criteria), slide 42 (O₂ titration with exercise), slide 65 (desaturation event / ODI). Related: RCP 203 Lesson 3b Ch 5 — Recommend Diagnostic Procedures, slide 33 (lab PSG indicated in COPD with awake PaO₂ > 55 torr plus pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure, polycythemia, or EDS).

records.item_title: LTOT — long-term oxygen therapy qualifying criteria (PaO₂ and SpO₂ thresholds)
records.quote: The same SpO₂ 88% / PaO₂ 55 torr pair is the decision point used during oxygen titration with exercise : if at peak activity the patient holds SpO₂ ≥ 88% (PaO₂ ≥ 55 torr) , no additional O₂ is needed and the test is terminated; if the SpO₂ drops by ≥ 2% OR falls below 88% (PaO₂ < 55 torr) , increase O₂ by 1 L/min until SpO₂ ≥ 88% .
records.cite: RCP 203 Lesson 3a Ch 4 — Evaluate Procedure Results, slide 66 (LTOT + nocturnal O₂ criteria), slide 42 (O₂ titration with exercise), slide 65 (desaturation event / ODI). Related: RCP 203 Lesson 3b Ch 5 — Recommend Diagnostic Procedures, slide 33 (lab PSG indicated in COPD with awake PaO₂ > 55 torr plus pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure, polycythemia, or EDS).

records.item_title: LTOT — long-term oxygen therapy qualifying criteria (PaO₂ and SpO₂ thresholds)
records.quote: Medicare reimburses nocturnal O₂ therapy when nocturnal oximetry demonstrates a > 5% drop in SpO₂ or an SpO₂ less than 88% , and the patient has signs or symptoms of hypoxemia (e.g., impaired cognitive process, insomnia) — criteria the deck notes are basically the same as the continuous LTOT criteria .
records.cite: RCP 203 Lesson 3a Ch 4 — Evaluate Procedure Results, slide 66 (LTOT + nocturnal O₂ criteria), slide 42 (O₂ titration with exercise), slide 65 (desaturation event / ODI). Related: RCP 203 Lesson 3b Ch 5 — Recommend Diagnostic Procedures, slide 33 (lab PSG indicated in COPD with awake PaO₂ > 55 torr plus pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure, polycythemia, or EDS).

records.item_title: LTOT — long-term oxygen therapy qualifying criteria (PaO₂ and SpO₂ thresholds)
records.quote: Setting Qualifying threshold Continuous LTOT in COPD SaO₂ ≤ 88% or PaO₂ ≤ 55 torr on room air Nocturnal O₂ (Medicare) > 5% drop in SpO₂ , or SpO₂ < 88% , plus signs/symptoms of hypoxemia O₂ titration during exercise — no O₂ needed SpO₂ ≥ 88% (PaO₂ ≥ 55 torr) at peak activity → terminate test O₂ titration during exercise — titrate up ↓ SpO₂ ≥ 2% OR SpO₂ < 88% (PaO₂ < 55 torr) → ↑ O₂ by 1 L/min until SpO₂ ≥ 88% Related sleep thresholds from the same chapter: a desaturation event is an SpO₂ drop of 4% or more ; the Oxygen Desaturation Index (ODI) is the average number of desaturation events per hour of sleep, and an ODI of 15 or more indicates Sleep Apnea–Hypopnea Syndrome (SAHS) .
records.cite: RCP 203 Lesson 3a Ch 4 — Evaluate Procedure Results, slide 66 (LTOT + nocturnal O₂ criteria), slide 42 (O₂ titration with exercise), slide 65 (desaturation event / ODI). Related: RCP 203 Lesson 3b Ch 5 — Recommend Diagnostic Procedures, slide 33 (lab PSG indicated in COPD with awake PaO₂ > 55 torr plus pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure, polycythemia, or EDS).

records.item_title: Oxygen therapy in COPD — the target the deck does give
records.quote: 20 Oxygen therapy in COPD — the target the deck does give The COPD oxygen protocol targets an SpO₂ of about 88–92% .
records.cite: COPD PP, slide 28

records.item_title: COPD therapist-driven protocols (TDPs)
records.quote: Oxygen protocol : target SpO₂ 88–92% as above.
records.cite: COPD PP, slides 28-29, 33; Ch 6 Adrenergics, slide 5

records.item_title: Worked case — putting the numbers together
records.quote: 23 Worked case — putting the numbers together A 78-year-old male with COPD diagnosed ~15 years ago, still smoking 2–3 packs/day , out of medications for 2 months , baseline FEV₁/FVC 55% , FEV₁ 35% predicted (GOLD 3) , mMRC 3 , DLCO 60% , 2 exacerbations in 12 months.
records.cite: COPD PP, slides 30-34

records.item_title: Worked case — putting the numbers together
records.quote: ABG on 2 L/min NC: pH 7.24, PaCO₂ 110, HCO₃⁻ 46, PaO₂ 47, SaO₂ 77% = acute on chronic ventilatory failure with moderate–severe hypoxemia.
records.cite: COPD PP, slides 30-34

records.item_title: ETT Sizes — Adult and Pediatric
records.quote: That is why 1 mm of circumferential edema is tolerated in an adult but can cut an infant's airway diameter by more than 50% .
records.cite: Airway Mngmnt (Hess Ch 17), slides 22, 34, 42 (notes), 39 Not in the deck: the pediatric ETT size formula (commonly taught as (age ÷ 4) + 4 for uncuffed, (age ÷ 4) + 3.5 for cuffed) and any pediatric depth-of-insertion rule. Look these up in the Chang neonatal/pediatric chapter — the airway deck only points to "Chang, Chapter 6" for ETT selection and never reproduces the table.

records.item_title: Cuff Pressure — The Number to Memorize
records.quote: The reason for the ceiling: tracheal capillary perfusion pressure is normally 25 to 35 mm Hg , and because the pressure transmitted from the cuff to the tracheal wall is usually less than the pressure inside the cuff, 30 cm H₂O is the maximum acceptable intracuff pressure — above that you risk mucosal ischemia, tracheal wall necrosis, and stenosis .
records.cite: Airway Mngmnt (Hess Ch 17), slides 86, 87, 88, 101

records.item_title: Cuff Pressure — The Number to Memorize
records.quote: 1 mmHg = 1.36 cmH₂O , or 1 cmH₂O ≈ 0.735 mmHg ), that range is roughly 14.7 to 22.05 mm Hg , and the deck adds that cuff pressure should stay < 25 mm Hg , and lower than 25 mm Hg if the patient is hypotensive .
records.cite: Airway Mngmnt (Hess Ch 17), slides 86, 87, 88, 101

records.item_title: Cuff Types and the Two Inflation Techniques
records.quote: Used properly, foam-cuff lateral tracheal wall pressure rarely exceeds 20 mm Hg (27 cm H₂O) .
records.cite: Airway Mngmnt (Hess Ch 17), slides 72, 86, 87

records.item_title: Mallampati Classification
records.quote: The deck's warning is important: given a roughly 10% incidence of difficult airways in hospital intubations, the value of these tools is their positive predictive value , and a reassuring score never excuses skipping a backup airway plan .
records.cite: RCP 103 — Clinical Data PP, slide 28 (full class-by-class structures); RCP 203 Lesson 2a Ch 2 — Perform Clinical Assessment, slides 23–24 (assessment sequence + difficulty ranking + Class IV/sleep apnea link); Sleep Apnea deck, slides 15 and 23 (Mallampati as OSA screening tool; score 3 or 4 ); RCP 105 Wk 1 Lecture 2 — Airway Management (Hess Ch 17), slide 26 (Figure 17-13). Source (MACOCHA and bedside difficult-airway signs): Airway Mngmnt (Hess Ch 17), slides 25, 26, 29 (notes), 36 (notes)

records.item_title: Rapid Sequence Intubation — The Three Phases
records.quote: Pretreatment is given about 3 to 5 minutes before the rest.
records.cite: Airway Mngmnt (Hess Ch 17), slides 42, 43 (notes), 44 (notes)

records.item_title: Rapid Sequence Intubation — The Three Phases
records.quote: Intubation is performed 30 to 60 seconds after the paralytic , when full paralysis is achieved.
records.cite: Airway Mngmnt (Hess Ch 17), slides 42, 43 (notes), 44 (notes)

records.item_title: The VAP Bundle
records.quote: 8 The VAP Bundle Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP) is pneumonia that develops 48 hours or more after endotracheal intubation and initiation of mechanical ventilation .
records.cite: RCP 105 Wk 5 — Procedures Related to Mechanical Ventilation (Chang Ch 14/15), slides 43–47 (slide 43 definition/epidemiology, slide 44 clinical presentation, slide 45 CPIS/BAL/PSB, slide 46 = the prevention bundle , slide 47 = the prevention summary table). Source (tube-design prevention): Airway Mngmnt (Hess Ch 17), slides 32 (notes), 86, 95 ⚠ Note the deck's own caveats: the printed bundle items #2 (circuits every 7 days) and #3 (inline suction/HME every 24 hours) are explicitly flagged in the speaker notes as outdated — current guidance is do NOT change circuits on a routine schedule; change only when visibly soiled or malfunctioning , because unnecessary circuit changes increase contamination. Silver-coated ETTs are not routinely used today. Report both the printed bundle and the update.

records.item_title: The VAP Bundle
records.quote: It affects 10 to 25% of mechanically ventilated patients, accounts for roughly 25% of all ICU-acquired infections , and carries a mortality of 33 to 50% ; the incidence in the first 5 days is 3% , and the single greatest risk factor is prolonged mechanical ventilation .
records.cite: RCP 105 Wk 5 — Procedures Related to Mechanical Ventilation (Chang Ch 14/15), slides 43–47 (slide 43 definition/epidemiology, slide 44 clinical presentation, slide 45 CPIS/BAL/PSB, slide 46 = the prevention bundle , slide 47 = the prevention summary table). records.item_title: The VAP Bundle

records.item_title: The VAP Bundle
records.quote: Additional deck-listed prevention methods good hand hygiene or gloves ( "by far the simplest and most cost-effective way to reduce the incidence of VAP" ); elevate the head of the bed 30–45 degrees at all times ( contraindicated after neurosurgery or with severe hypotension ); change the ventilator circuit when visibly soiled ; use noninvasive ventilation to avoid an artificial airway altogether; schedule a sedative vacation 6 to 8 hours daily ; early weaning from mechanical ventilation ; decontamination of the oropharynx / oral chlorhexidine ; use of an oral (not nasal) feeding tube ; aspiration precautions ;

records.item_title: The VAP Bundle
records.quote: "The single best way to prevent VAP is early liberation from mechanical ventilation whenever it is safe to do so." records.item_title: The Clean Distinction — Ventilation is CO₂, Oxygenation is O₂
records.quote: The ABG deck states it directly when listing why we draw an arterial sample — "to determine the adequacy of the patient's ventilation (PaCO₂) , oxygenation (PaO₂) , and acid-base status (pH) ." Ventilation is about moving air in and out to clear CO₂ ; when it fails you get hypoventilation → ↑ PaCO₂ → respiratory acidosis , and the deck calls that ventilatory failure , defined as PaCO₂ > 45 mm Hg with pH < 7.35 .
records.cite: ABG Assessments (RCP 103), slides 16, 50 (notes), 17; Principles of Mech Vent (Chang/Hess), slides 20, 25

records.item_title: The Clean Distinction — Ventilation is CO₂, Oxygenation is O₂
records.quote: Oxygenation is about getting O₂ from the alveolus into the blood and on to the tissues ; when it fails you get hypoxemia , and oxygenation failure is defined as severe hypoxemia (PaO₂ < 40 mm Hg) in spite of a high FiO₂ (50% to 100%) .
records.cite: ABG Assessments (RCP 103), slides 16, 50 (notes), 17; Principles of Mech Vent (Chang/Hess), slides 20, 25

records.item_title: The Clean Distinction — Ventilation is CO₂, Oxygenation is O₂
records.quote: The deck's own worked example: an opioid overdose with PaCO₂ 105 mm Hg, pH 7.14, PaO₂ 36 mm Hg is a ventilation problem first.
records.cite: ABG Assessments (RCP 103), slides 16, 50 (notes), 17; Principles of Mech Vent (Chang/Hess), slides 20, 25

records.item_title: Hypoxemia vs. Hypoxia — Not the Same Word
records.quote: Hypoxia — Not the Same Word Hypoxemia = low oxygen in the BLOOD (a blood-oxygen problem, measured by PaO₂ and SaO₂ ; e.g., PaO₂ = 50 mm Hg ).
records.cite: Principles of Mech Vent (Chang/Hess), slides 25 (notes), 26

records.item_title: Hypoxemia vs. Hypoxia — Not the Same Word
records.quote: Normal hemoglobin for reference: adult men 13.5 to 17.5 g/dL , adult women 12.0 to 15.5 g/dL .
records.cite: Principles of Mech Vent (Chang/Hess), slides 25 (notes), 26

records.item_title: Normal Blood Gas Values
records.quote: Arterial: pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO₂ 35–45 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 22–28 mEq/L (NBRC uses 22–26), PaO₂ 80–100 mm Hg, base excess −2 to +2 mEq/L.
records.cite: ABG Assessments (RCP 103), slides 4, 12, 13, 70 (notes)

records.item_title: Normal Blood Gas Values
records.quote: Venous: pH 7.30–7.40, PaCO₂ 42–48 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 24–30 mEq/L, PaO₂ 35–45 mm Hg, BE −2 to +2 mEq/L.
records.cite: ABG Assessments (RCP 103), slides 4, 12, 13, 70 (notes)

records.item_title: Normal Blood Gas Values
records.quote: Two other thresholds worth memorizing from this deck: peripheral chemoreceptors fire when PaO₂ falls to about 60 mm Hg , triggering hyperventilation, and in COPD a PaO₂ around 55–60 mm Hg can be acceptable .
records.cite: ABG Assessments (RCP 103), slides 4, 12, 13, 70 (notes)

records.item_title: The Four Causes of Ventilatory / Respiratory Failure

records.item_title: Dead Space — Anatomic, Alveolar, and Physiologic
records.quote: Anatomic dead space is the conducting airways ( nose, mouth, trachea, bronchi ) and the rule to memorize is 1 mL per pound of body weight — so a 150 lb person has about 150 mL of anatomic dead space.
records.cite: Principles of Mech Vent (Chang/Hess), slides 15, 16, 17, 18 Not stated explicitly in the deck: a normal VD/VT range . The only figure the deck supplies is the 30% in its own 500 mL example (commonly taught as 20–40% , or ~1/3 of each breath). Confirm the range in your gas-exchange chapter.

records.item_title: Dead Space vs. Shunt — The One-Line Discriminator

records.item_title: Quantifying Oxygenation — The A-a Gradient
records.quote: PAO₂ = FiO₂ × (Pb − PH₂O) − (PaCO₂ / RQ) , where Pb ≈ 760 mm Hg at sea level , PH₂O ≈ 47 mm Hg at body temperature , RQ ≈ 0.8 , and FiO₂ = 0.21 on room air, 1.0 on 100% O₂ .
records.cite: Principles of Mech Vent (Chang/Hess), slide 24

records.item_title: Quantifying Oxygenation — The A-a Gradient
records.quote: P(A–a)O₂ = (1000 − PaCO₂/0.8) − PaO₂ , with the warning that this is only an approximation valid when the patient is on 100% oxygen .
records.cite: Principles of Mech Vent (Chang/Hess), slide 24

records.item_title: Quantifying Oxygenation — The A-a Gradient
records.quote: 5–15 mm Hg in a young adult on room air , increasing with age by the rough estimate [Age ÷ 4] + 4 , and up to 100–200 mm Hg is acceptable on 100% O₂ .
records.cite: Principles of Mech Vent (Chang/Hess), slide 24

records.item_title: Quantifying Ventilation — What a PaCO₂ Change Does to pH
records.quote: Working from the baseline pH 7.40 / PaCO₂ 40 / HCO₃⁻ 24 : for every 10 mm Hg rise in PaCO₂ , pH falls about 0.06 and HCO₃⁻ rises about 1 mEq/L ; for every 20 mm Hg rise , pH falls 0.12 and HCO₃⁻ rises 2 mEq/L .
records.cite: ABG Assessments (RCP 103), slides 7, 8, 9, 18, 20, 22

records.item_title: Quantifying Ventilation — What a PaCO₂ Change Does to pH
records.quote: PaCO₂ 40 → 60 gives an expected pH ≈ 7.28 and HCO₃⁻ ≈ 26 mEq/L .
records.cite: ABG Assessments (RCP 103), slides 7, 8, 9, 18, 20, 22

records.item_title: Quantifying Ventilation — What a PaCO₂ Change Does to pH
records.quote: Chronic changes are different because renal compensation takes 3 to 5 days : for every 10 mm Hg rise in PaCO₂ , HCO₃⁻ rises about 3.5–4 mEq/L , and for every 10 mm Hg fall , HCO₃⁻ drops about 4–5 mEq/L .
records.cite: ABG Assessments (RCP 103), slides 7, 8, 9, 18, 20, 22

records.item_title: Transmission-Based Precautions
records.quote: 1 Transmission-Based Precautions ≈ 3 feet DROPLET > 5 µm — falls fast AIRBORNE ≤ 5 µm — stays suspended crosses rooms → N95 + neg. pressure Settling behaviour, not infectivity, is what separates the two categories — and it is why one needs proximity and the other needs engineering controls.

records.quote: "If the aerosol mist disappears during inspiration in a patient receiving O2 via a large-volume nebulizer and T-piece or mask, the flow is inadequate." The fixes, in Heuer's order: maximize input flow ; add an open reservoir to the expiratory side of the T-tube ; connect multiple nebulizers in parallel ; provide an inspiratory reservoir with a one-way expiratory valve ; set the nebulizer to a low O2% and bleed in extra O2 .

records.item_title: Briggs Adaptor (T-Piece)
records.quote: Deck contribution The decks define the Briggs adaptor from the weaning side: a spontaneous breathing trial (SBT) can be run with a T-piece (Briggs adapter) , with low-level pressure support (5–8 cm H2O to offset the ETT) , with CPAP (~5 cm H2O) , or with automatic tube compensation (ATC) — and all of these methods produce similar weaning outcomes .

records.item_title: Spirometry Calibration to ATS Standards
records.quote: Test Minimum interval Action / standard Leaks Daily 3 cm H2O constant pressure for 1 minute ; leak must be < 10 mL Volume Daily Calibration check with a 3-L syringe — ±3% or ±50 mL Volume linearity Quarterly 1-L increments with a calibrating syringe over the entire volume range Flow linearity Weekly Test at at least three different flow ranges Time Quarterly Mechanical recorder checked against a stopwatch Software New versions Log the install date and test a known subject ("biological control") Leak check detail (volumetric bell/bellows spirometers), done daily BEFORE the volume check and after any cleaning/reassembly: inject ~3 L of room air, occlude the circuit at the patient interface, pressurize to 3 cm H2O , and watch for volume change over 1 minute .

records.quote: A slow or false start — back-extrapolated volume ≥ 5% of FVC or 150 mL (produces a characteristic S-shaped curve, low slope early then steepening) Coughing during the maneuver Breathing during the maneuver (an extra breath shows as a short plateau; measured volume may overestimate the true FVC ) Variable effort — prematurely ending exhalation (curve ends abruptly in a plateau ) Exhalation time less than 6 seconds ATS repeatability/reproducibility criterion After acceptability, confirm reproducibility: the two largest values for BOTH the FVC and the FEV1 must be within 0.150 L (150 mL) of each other.

records.quote: Avoidance: analyze within 30 minutes in a plastic syringe ( 3 minutes for capillary ), immediately with a high leukocyte or platelet count (those cells consume O2 and generate CO2 fastest), and for storage > 30 minutes use a glass syringe chilled to 0–4°C — chilling slows cellular metabolism and preserves the values.

records.item_title: Transcutaneous Monitoring (PtcO2 / PtcCO2)
records.quote: Setup procedure Membrane the sensor and calibrate per the manufacturer's instructions → set the proper temperature → choose a site with good superficial circulation ( side of the chest, below the clavicles, the abdomen, the inner thigh ) and clean it with alcohol → apply the adhesive fixation ring → apply contact gel to the sensor face and inside the ring, avoiding air bubbles → apply the sensor flat with the edges sealed → allow 5–20 minutes for the reading to stabilize → set alarms ( high PtcO2 for infants typically 80 torr ).

records.item_title: QC on Mechanical Ventilators and on Gas Analyzers
records.quote: Component checked Standard / procedure Battery / power-loss alarm Disconnect then reconnect power with the unit on — battery backup and disconnect alarms must function FiO2 / O2 analyzer Verified using the O2 analyzer two-point calibration in item 3 above Gas supply alarms Disconnect the high-pressure O2 hose, then separately the air hose — the appropriate alarms must sound Apnea alarm Test lung, SIMV rate = 2/min , trigger 8–12 times , then stop triggering and confirm the alarm High-pressure alarm Momentarily occlude the circuit and confirm audible + visual alarms Proximal airway pressure display Disconnect the pressure line — display must read zero (±1 cm H2O) .

records.item_title: QC on Mechanical Ventilators and on Gas Analyzers
records.quote: At PEEP 10 cm H2O , pressure must return to baseline (±1 cm H2O) each breath PEEP control Set 5 cm H2O , confirm return to 5 (±1 cm H2O) ; repeat at 10 and 15 cm H2O Leak test — occlusion method Occlude the patient connection, pressure limit at maximum , peak flow at minimum , deliver a 200–300 mL breath (adults) — the pressure limit should be reached and the high-pressure alarm activate Leak test — plateau pressure method Set an inspiratory pause ≥ 2 seconds ; a drop of 10% or more during the pause indicates a leak Ventilator rate Count breaths against a watch — measured rate must be within one breath per minute of the set rate and the rate display Delivered volume Connect a respirometer to the ventilator outlet — all measurements within ±5% of the set volume Sensitivity In assist mode, squeezing and releasing the test lung must trigger a breath at the set sensitivity level Filters Confirm a HEPA filter on the main inspiratory line (Heuer's T4 tip condenses the leak test: use the occlusion method — max pressure limit, low flow and volume — to verify the high-pressure alarm, or verify a < 10% pressure drop during a prolonged inspiratory pause .) records.quote: (RCP 203 gives the same 30–120 min ; the Chang Weaning deck says "up to 30 minutes" via ventilator or Briggs adaptor/T-tube , and notes patients who fail usually do so within the first 20–30 minutes , so a full 120-minute trial is often unnecessary.) records.item_title: Making Ventilator Changes from an ABG
records.quote: His decision rule is the "60-60 rule" (a "50-50 rule" works too): if PaO2 > 60 torr on FiO2 < 0.6, the problem is V/Q imbalance → simply raise the FiO2; if PaO2 < 60 torr on FiO2 > 0.6, the problem is shunt → PEEP/CPAP must be added or increased.

records.item_title: PIP, Pplat, PEEP — Normal Levels, Body Effects, and Auto-PEEP
records.quote: Decremental PEEP study (Box 11-3): switch to VC at VT 4–6 mL/kg PBW , start from the RM PEEP ( 20–25 ), drop PEEP in 2-cmH2O steps allowing 3–5 minutes between steps , measuring Crs = VT ÷ (Pplat − PEEP) each time, continue until you pass the highest Crs (you must see at least one decrease from the peak) , repeat the recruitment , then set PEEP 2 cmH2O above the level that gave the highest Crs , and check a blood gas after 20–30 minutes.

records.item_title: Pressure-Volume and Flow-Volume Loops
records.quote: Heuer is specific — "PEEP typically is set 2–3 cmH2O above the LIP." The point is to reduce the opening-pressure requirement, minimize alveolar collapse during expiration, improve recruitment and oxygenation, and reduce repetitive opening and closing (atelectrauma).

records.item_title: Pressure-Volume and Flow-Volume Loops
records.quote: Type What to look for Corrective actions Ineffective trigger pressure and flow scalars show a delayed or absent response to the patient's effort (e.g., the patient must drop the pressure 10 cmH2O below baseline to trigger) Increase sensitivity; switch to flow triggering; reduce/counteract auto-PEEP; reduce sedation Autocycling extra breaths triggered without patient effort , usually from circuit condensate or leaks Decrease sensitivity; switch to flow triggering; correct leaks; drain condensate and change filters Double triggering two consecutive machine breaths with no interval between them ↑ inspiratory flow (VC); ↑ set VT (VC); ↑ inspiratory time (PC); shorten rise time (PC); ↑ pressure level (PS); ↓ %cycling criteria (PS) Inadequate flow (flow starvation) "scalloping" / concavity in the pressure scalar of assisted breaths, or on the flow scalar during volume ventilation ↑ flow (VC); change flow pattern (VC); switch VC to PC; ↑ set PIP (PC); shorten rise time (PC); find and correct the cause of increased ventilatory demand Excessive flow pressure peak achieved too early (PC) , or an upward spike on inspiratory flow (VC) ↓ inspiratory flow (VC); ↓ set PIP (PC); lengthen rise time (PC)

records.quote: Cuff pressure target = 20 - 30 cm H2O (30 cm H2O = maximum intracuff) 25 cm H2O = typical hospital / NBRC high-pressure limit Convert cm H2O -> mm Hg : mm Hg = cm H2O / 1.36 (1 mm Hg = 1.36 cm H2O) 20 / 1.36 = 14.7 mm Hg 30 / 1.36 = 22.0 mm Hg Tracheal capillary perfusion pressure = 25 - 35 mm Hg -> keep cuff < 25 mm Hg; go lower still if the patient is hypotensive Too small a tube -> more air needed to seal -> higher wall pressure -> ischemia Fix = exchange for a larger tube, NOT more air

records.item_title: How a CXR Relates to Palpation, Percussion, and Breath Sounds
records.quote: Heart failure on CXR: cardiomegaly (CT ratio > 50% on a PA film) , prominent upper-lobe vascular markings , Kerley B lines , and pleural effusions .

records.item_title: Tracheal Shift, Paradoxical Breathing, and Flail Chest
records.quote: Standard approach when ventilation IS needed: intubation + A/C mode (VC, PCV, PRVC, or bilevel) with PEEP ; try mask CPAP or BiPAP first in an alert, cooperative patient with marginal status Watch for Associated pulmonary contusion — its full effects may not appear for 24-48 hours , so admit and monitor for worsening hypoxemia and ARDS .
records.cite: Heuer Ch 2 — Tracheal Position (PDF p113), Table 2-7 (p100); Ch 15 — Treating a Tension Pneumothorax (p701) and T4 Tips (p721); Ch 20 — Chest Trauma, Table 20-4 · RCP 203 Lssn 2a, slides 11, 39, 50 · RCP 105 Wk 1 Lctr 4 — Operating Modes, slide 15

records.item_title: Orthopnea — Definition, Meaning, Quantifying It, and the Workup
records.quote: Test Numbers What it tells you BNP Heuer: reference < 20 pg/mL ; < 100 pg/mL rules OUT CHF; > 500 pg/mL rules IN CHF ⚠ Deck: normal < 100 , 100-300 = HF may be present, > 300 mild, > 600 moderate, > 900 severe Distinguishes a cardiac cause of SOB (CHF) from a pulmonary one (COPD) Troponin I Heuer: < 0.4 μg/L ; rises 3-6 hr after insult, peaks at 12 hr , persists 7 days ⚠ Deck: normal < 0.1 ng/mL AMI / acute coronary syndrome CK-MB < 4-6% of total CK; rises 4-6 hr , peaks at 24 hr , normal in 2-3 days AMI CXR CT ratio > 50% on a PA film = cardiomegaly Heart failure vs. primary lung disease: cardiomegaly , prominent upper-lobe vascular markings , Kerley B lines , pleural effusions Echocardiogram — Cardiac structure and function ; systolic HF shows decreased LV function 12-lead ECG — Rhythm, ischemia , infarction
records.cite: Heuer Ch 2 — Breathing Difficulties and Exercise Tolerance (PDF p89), Table 2-7 (p97-98); Ch 1 — Table 1-3 Laboratory Reference Ranges (p43), Heart Size on CXR (Ch 2, p123-124) · RCP 203 Lssn 2a, slides 10-11 · RCP 103 Clinical Data PP, slides 17, 48, 54, 60

records.item_title: Breathing Patterns
records.quote: 6 Breathing Patterns Pattern Description Cause Eupnea Normal rate and depth Normal baseline Orthopnea Breathlessness lying flat , relieved by sitting/standing; patient is "always elevated with pillows" CHF , fluid overload, various cardiac and pulmonary disorders Tachypnea Fast RR (> 20/min) Respiratory distress , restrictive disease , hypoxemia, fever, pain, anxiety, ↑ metabolic rate (fever, infection) Bradypnea Slow RR (< 12/min) Sleep (normal), oversedation , ↓ PaCO₂ , ↓ metabolic rate, hypothermia , respiratory failure/arrest — reverse sedation or support Apnea No breathing Respiratory or cardiac arrest , severe CNS failure Kussmaul Deep AND fast respirations Metabolic acidosis , classically diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) — blowing off CO₂.

records.quote: Heuer Table 2-7 also lists mottled/acrocyanotic skin When it appears With normal Hb, generally first appears when SaO₂ drops below 80% ( PaO₂ 45-50 torr ) Can occur with a completely normal SaO₂ Paired finding Arterial hypoxemia With cool extremities and capillary refill ≥ 3 seconds → circulatory failure Why anemia masks it the sign depends on an absolute amount of desaturated hemoglobin, not a percentage.

records.quote: Management is high-quality CPR + epinephrine 1 mg IV every 3-5 minutes with a flush (vasoconstrictor; improves cerebral perfusion ).

records.item_title: PEA — Pulseless Electrical Activity, and the H's and T's
records.quote: Capnography is now a standard of care during resuscitation: if PetCO₂ < 10 mm Hg and intra-arterial diastolic pressure < 20 mm Hg , the quality of CPR must be improved ; failure to achieve PetCO₂ > 10 mm Hg after 20 minutes of CPR can be used as an indicator to terminate resuscitation.
