records.item_title: PFTs — When and How, the Bronchodilator-Response Threshold, and Spirometry Hazards
records.quote: PERCENT PREDICTED = (actual ÷ predicted) × 100 HEUER WORKED EXAMPLE (App B, Problem B.19) Measured FVC 3.25 L, predicted normal FVC 3.82 L % predicted = 3.25 ÷ 3.82 × 100 = 85% of normal PERCENT CHANGE = [(post − pre) ÷ pre] × 100 HEUER WORKED EXAMPLE #1 (App B, Problem B.18) Pre-bronchodilator FEV1 = 2.4 L Post-bronchodilator FEV1 = 2.7 L (2.7 − 2.4) ÷ 2.4 = 0.3 ÷ 2.4 = 0.125 0.125 × 100 = 12.5% → MEETS the 12–15% bar (borderline positive) HEUER WORKED EXAMPLE #2 (Ch 4, PDF p245 — same numbers as the deck) Pre FEV1 = 3.0 L Post FEV1 = 3.3 L (3.3 − 3.0) ÷ 3.0 = 0.3 ÷ 3.0 = 0.10 0.10 × 100 = 10% → NOT a significant response THE BRONCHODILATOR-RESPONSE THRESHOLD — "AND" vs "OR" IS A REAL CONFLICT.

records.item_title: Single-Breath N2 Washout — What It Measures and the Four Phases
records.quote: The single-breath technique Heuer does detail is the single-breath DLCO : exhale to RV , inhale to TLC a mix of 21% O2, 10% He, 0.3% CO , 10-second breath-hold , discard the first (anatomic dead space) portion, then collect 0.5–1.0 L of expired gas for % He and % CO ; repeat after ≥ 4 minutes until results agree within 5% or 3 mL/min/mm Hg .

records.quote: Neuro-Respiratory Disorders deck Normal range −60 to −100 cm H2O ; weaker than −30 = severe inspiratory muscle weakness (e.g. an MIP of −15 confirms inadequate ability to sustain ventilation ) Neuro-Respiratory Disorders deck Weaning readiness: −20 to −30 cm H2O generated in 20 sec RCP 105 Wk 3 Weaning, slide 16 Weaning likely successful if MIP is at least −30 cm H2O ; across 11 studies MIP averaged −37 cm H2O in weaned vs −30 cm H2O in non-weaned patients RCP 105 Wk 3 Weaning, slide 15 Note the normal-value conflict Heuer says normal MIP is −80 to −100 (agreeing with the weaning deck), while Lssn 2b slide 19 says "normal NIF is > −60." records.item_title: Inspiratory Flow Demand — How to Calculate It
records.quote: Raw = ΔP ÷ V̇ where ΔP = PIP − Pplat and V̇ = inspiratory flow (L/sec) Crs (static compliance) = VT ÷ (Pplat − PEEP) Cdyn = VT ÷ (PIP − PEEP) Cdyn is ALWAYS less than Crs; the gap is Raw Normal Raw (deck) = 0.6–2.4 cm H2O/L/sec (≈ 1–3) Heuer (Ch 1) = values above 5–9 cm H2O/L/sec are associated with obstruction Deck thresholds = Raw > 5 → airway obstruction Raw > 10 → severe bronchospasm, mucus plugging, kinked/obstructed ETT Heuer adds: an ETT itself adds at least 4–6 cm H2O/L/sec to total resistance.

records.item_title: Capnography: how to measure; difference between waveforms, sudden increases or decreases
records.quote: Change in ETCO2 Possible causes (per the decks) Sudden drop to zero Ventilator/circuit disconnection (immediate disappearance of values and waveform); complete ET tube obstruction/kink ; esophageal intubation (no waveform — waveform capnography is the gold standard for confirming tracheal placement) Sudden decrease (not to zero) Cardiac arrest / falling cardiac output — values drop suddenly and proportionally because lung perfusion is inadequate; partial ET tube obstruction or kink ; increased alveolar deadspace (e.g., pulmonary embolism) — this is not an improvement in ventilation, so do not lower the ventilator rate Gradual increase Hypoventilation trend (rising PaCO2 — confirm with ABG); increased CO2 production / rising metabolic rate ; a baseline that rises off zero indicates rebreathing in the circuit Gradual decrease Hyperventilation trend (falling PaCO2 — confirm with ABG); rising physiologic deadspace / worsening V/Q ; falling cardiac output or lung perfusion (during CPR, PETCO2 < 10 torr means poor or absent pulmonary blood flow; a rise in PETCO2 signals effective compressions or ROSC )

records.item_title: Explain Hemodynamic Measurements; CVP and PA Catheters — normal ranges
records.quote: 30–50% = onset of lactic acidosis, 25–30% = severe lactic acidosis, < 25% = cellular death .
records.cite: Chang Ch.10 – Hemodynamic Monitoring, slides 3–5, 8–10, 12, 14–15, 19, 21, 23, 25–33; RCP 203 Lesson 2b (Chp 3), slide 33; RCP 103 – Clinical Data, slides 9, 12; Pulmonary Edema and PVD, slide 66

records.item_title: Pulmonary Artery Catheters – hemodynamic parameters
records.quote: It carries a distal PA port at the tip , a proximal injectate port about 30 cm back (sits in the right atrium) , a balloon near the tip with a 1.5 mL maximum inflation volume , and a thermistor at the tip; a fiberoptic element allows continuous SvO2 .
records.cite: Chang Ch.10 – Hemodynamic Monitoring, slides 11, 16–19, 21–23, 25; RCP 203 Lesson 2b (Chp 3), slides 33–35

records.item_title: Pulmonary Artery Catheters – hemodynamic parameters
records.quote: 10 mL of iced or room-temperature D5W is injected into the proximal port and the temperature change at the thermistor is used to compute flow.
records.cite: Chang Ch.10 – Hemodynamic Monitoring, slides 11, 16–19, 21–23, 25; RCP 203 Lesson 2b (Chp 3), slides 33–35

records.item_title: Difference between Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) and Intracranial Pressure (ICP)
records.quote: The formula the RCP 203 deck gives is MAP = Diastolic + 1/3 (Systolic − Diastolic) ; worked example, 110/70 → 70 + 1/3(40) = 70 + 13.3 ≈ 83 mm Hg .
records.cite: Chang Ch.9 – Monitoring in Mechanical Ventilation, slides 38, 52–54; Chang Ch.10 – Hemodynamic Monitoring, slide 8; RCP 203 Lesson 3a (Chp 4), slide 46

records.item_title: Difference between Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) and Intracranial Pressure (ICP)
records.quote: The decks do not print a single "normal MAP range," but they give the clinical thresholds : a MAP of 60 mm Hg is needed to maintain tissue perfusion , and a MAP of 70 mm Hg is needed to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure .
records.cite: Chang Ch.9 – Monitoring in Mechanical Ventilation, slides 38, 52–54; Chang Ch.10 – Hemodynamic Monitoring, slide 8; RCP 203 Lesson 3a (Chp 4), slide 46

records.item_title: Difference between Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) and Intracranial Pressure (ICP)
records.quote: Normal ICP is < 20 mm Hg.
records.cite: Chang Ch.9 – Monitoring in Mechanical Ventilation, slides 38, 52–54; Chang Ch.10 – Hemodynamic Monitoring, slide 8; RCP 203 Lesson 3a (Chp 4), slide 46

records.item_title: Difference between Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) and Intracranial Pressure (ICP)
records.quote: The critical CPP threshold is ≥ 70 mm Hg (believed to be 70–80 mm Hg ); mortality increases about 20% for every 10 mm Hg drop in CPP , and in severe head injury a 35% reduction in mortality was achieved when CPP was kept above 70 mm Hg .
records.cite: Chang Ch.9 – Monitoring in Mechanical Ventilation, slides 38, 52–54; Chang Ch.10 – Hemodynamic Monitoring, slide 8; RCP 203 Lesson 3a (Chp 4), slide 46

records.item_title: Difference between Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) and Intracranial Pressure (ICP)
records.quote: ICP control is generally unnecessary when ICP is already < 20 mm Hg , but is necessary in closed head injuries .
records.cite: Chang Ch.9 – Monitoring in Mechanical Ventilation, slides 38, 52–54; Chang Ch.10 – Hemodynamic Monitoring, slide 8; RCP 203 Lesson 3a (Chp 4), slide 46

records.item_title: Diuretics and their role
records.quote: Very weak diuretics ; used to treat metabolic alkalosis , altitude sickness, glaucoma Loop ("high-ceiling") — furosemide (Lasix) , bumetanide, torsemide, ethacrynic acid Ascending loop of Henle — inhibits Na+/K+/Cl− reabsorption ; blocks up to ~20% of NaCl and H2O Hypokalemia (most important — can cause arrhythmias) , hypochloremia , metabolic alkalosis , hypovolemia/hypotension , calcium loss , dose-related ototoxicity (tinnitus, usually reversible hearing loss) Thiazides — hydrochlorothiazide class Distal tubule — inhibits NaCl reabsorption Hypokalemia (milder), mild volume depletion , hyperglycemia — thiazides have the strongest diabetogenic activity (DKA reported).

records.item_title: Explain Transcutaneous Monitoring – electrode placement, troubleshooting
records.quote: 44°C is the usual setting when monitoring both PtcO2 and PtcCO2 , as low as 37°C is adequate if only PtcCO2 is monitored , and Chang states 44°C for PtcCO2 with 40–42°C in neonates, maximum 45°C .
records.cite: Chang Ch.9 – Monitoring in Mechanical Ventilation, slides 49–51; RCP 203 Lesson 2b (Chp 3), slides 11–12; RCP 203 Lesson 3a (Chp 4), slides 18–19; RCP 203 Lesson 3b (Chp 5), slide 21; RCP 203 Lesson 1 (Chp 1), slide 44

records.item_title: Explain Transcutaneous Monitoring – electrode placement, troubleshooting
records.quote: Placement: choose a site with good superficial circulation — the side of the chest, the abdomen, or the inner thigh — clean with alcohol , apply the adhesive fixation ring , apply contact gel to the sensor face avoiding air bubbles , seat the sensor flat with the edges sealed , and allow 5–20 minutes to stabilize .
records.cite: Chang Ch.9 – Monitoring in Mechanical Ventilation, slides 49–51; RCP 203 Lesson 2b (Chp 3), slides 11–12; RCP 203 Lesson 3a (Chp 4), slides 18–19; RCP 203 Lesson 3b (Chp 5), slide 21; RCP 203 Lesson 1 (Chp 1), slide 44

records.item_title: Explain Transcutaneous Monitoring – electrode placement, troubleshooting
records.quote: Burn risk drives site rotation: the decks conflict slightly — Chang says change the site every 4 hours to avoid erythema and burns; the RCP 203 procedure deck says every 2–6 hours depending on sensor temperature, infant size, and manufacturer recommendation .
records.cite: Chang Ch.9 – Monitoring in Mechanical Ventilation, slides 49–51; RCP 203 Lesson 2b (Chp 3), slides 11–12; RCP 203 Lesson 3a (Chp 4), slides 18–19; RCP 203 Lesson 3b (Chp 5), slide 21; RCP 203 Lesson 1 (Chp 1), slide 44

records.item_title: Explain Transcutaneous Monitoring – electrode placement, troubleshooting
records.quote: Population: it suits neonates and infants best — in neonates PtcO2 closely approximates PaO2 , keep PtcO2 in the 50–80 torr trend range (Chang: optimal 50–70 mm Hg ), set the high PtcO2 infant alarm around 80 torr , and infant PtcO2 is the best way to screen for hyperoxemia and help prevent retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) .
records.cite: Chang Ch.9 – Monitoring in Mechanical Ventilation, slides 49–51; RCP 203 Lesson 2b (Chp 3), slides 11–12; RCP 203 Lesson 3a (Chp 4), slides 18–19; RCP 203 Lesson 3b (Chp 5), slide 21; RCP 203 Lesson 1 (Chp 1), slide 44

records.item_title: Explain Transcutaneous Monitoring – electrode placement, troubleshooting
records.quote: PtcCO2 reads falsely high from tissue CO2 accumulation), skin edema , hypothermia , a PaO2 or operating range above 80–100 mm Hg , an underheated sensor , placement on a bony surface , too much pressure or too much contact gel , poor skin integrity or adhesive allergy , and the 5–20 minute setup time that rules it out in emergencies .
records.cite: Chang Ch.9 – Monitoring in Mechanical Ventilation, slides 49–51; RCP 203 Lesson 2b (Chp 3), slides 11–12; RCP 203 Lesson 3a (Chp 4), slides 18–19; RCP 203 Lesson 3b (Chp 5), slide 21; RCP 203 Lesson 1 (Chp 1), slide 44

records.item_title: Explain Transcutaneous Monitoring – electrode placement, troubleshooting
records.quote: Two extras: dual-sensor PtcO2 screens newborns for critical congenital heart disease (CCHD) — suspect it if the pre-ductal (right upper chest) PtcO2 is ≥ 15 torr higher than the post-ductal (lower abdomen/thigh) value — and wound-tissue PtcO2 > 30–40 torr indicates perfusion adequate for healing.
records.cite: Chang Ch.9 – Monitoring in Mechanical Ventilation, slides 49–51; RCP 203 Lesson 2b (Chp 3), slides 11–12; RCP 203 Lesson 3a (Chp 4), slides 18–19; RCP 203 Lesson 3b (Chp 5), slide 21; RCP 203 Lesson 1 (Chp 1), slide 44

records.item_title: Home Apnea Monitoring (conditions requiring its use)
records.quote: Most apnea monitors use two chest-wall sensors that detect respiratory movement by changes in electrical impedance , placed on the right and left sides of the chest, midway between the nipple line and the midaxillary line where chest motion is greatest; typical settings are a heart-rate alarm of 80–210/min for neonates (lower limits for older babies) and an apnea time alarm of 15–20 seconds .
records.cite: RCP 203 Lesson 2b (Chp 3), slides 46–48; RCP 203 Lesson 3a (Chp 4), slides 61–63

records.item_title: Home Apnea Monitoring (conditions requiring its use)
records.quote: Definitions to know: apnea = cessation of respiratory effort (short central pauses < 10 sec can be normal at any age); pathologic apnea = apnea longer than 20 seconds, or associated with cyanosis, abrupt marked pallor, hypotonia, or bradycardia (< 80–100 beats/min in neonates) ; periodic breathing = three or more pauses of > 3 seconds with < 20 seconds of breathing between them , which is not associated with cyanosis or heart-rate change and can be normal .
records.cite: RCP 203 Lesson 2b (Chp 3), slides 46–48; RCP 203 Lesson 3a (Chp 4), slides 61–63

records.item_title: How to Obtain an APGAR Score
records.quote: 1 How to Obtain an APGAR Score The Apgar score is taken on every newborn at 1 minute and again at 5 minutes after birth.
records.cite: RCP 203 Lssn 2a (Chp 2 – Perform Clinical Assessment), slide 28

records.item_title: How to Obtain an APGAR Score
records.quote: Component (mnemonic) What is being assessed Score range A — Appearance Color 0 / 1 / 2 P — Pulse Heart rate 0 / 1 / 2 G — Grimace Reflex irritability 0 / 1 / 2 A — Activity Muscle tone 0 / 1 / 2 R — Respirations Respiratory effort 0 / 1 / 2 Total Sum of all five 0–10 Timing Total score Interpretation 1 minute and 5 minutes after birth 7–10 Normal " 4–6 Moderately depressed — typically needs more intensive support " 0–3 Severely depressed — usually undergoes resuscitation ; requires immediate assessment/support Note: the deck names the five components and the 0–2 scale but does not print the individual 0/1/2 descriptor criteria (e.g., exact heart-rate cutoffs) for each row — look those up in the textbook table on p.40 if the exam asks for the specific descriptors.
records.cite: RCP 203 Lssn 2a (Chp 2 – Perform Clinical Assessment), slide 28

records.item_title: APGAR vs. Glasgow vs. Ballard vs. Silverman
records.quote: The critical clinical trigger is GCS ≤ 8 = intubate (consider the need for airway protection).
records.cite: RCP 203 Lssn 2a (Chp 2 – Perform Clinical Assessment), slides 8, 28, 29–30

records.item_title: APGAR vs. Glasgow vs. Ballard vs. Silverman
records.quote: Score What it assesses When used Scale / range Apgar Immediate newborn condition across 5 signs (Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respirations) At 1 min and 5 min after birth Each sign 0–2 ; total 0–10 ( 7–10 normal, 4–6 moderately depressed, 0–3 severely depressed) Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) Level of consciousness — eye , verbal , and motor responses Any patient with altered mentation / neurologic injury 3 (deep coma) to 15 (fully alert);
records.cite: RCP 203 Lssn 2a (Chp 2 – Perform Clinical Assessment), slides 8, 28, 29–30

records.item_title: APGAR vs. Glasgow vs. Ballard vs. Silverman
records.quote: 13–15 mild, 9–12 moderate, ≤ 8 severe/coma → intubate Ballard (Dubowitz/Ballard) Gestational age via neuromuscular + physical maturity characteristics After birth , once the infant can be examined (esp. premature infants) Total score converts to estimated gestational age in weeks (normal full term 38–42 wks ; term ≈ 37–42 wks ) Silverman Silverman-Anderson Index — objective scoring of neonatal respiratory distress , 5 features scored 0 / 1 / 2 (max 10 ).
records.cite: RCP 203 Lssn 2a (Chp 2 – Perform Clinical Assessment), slides 8, 28, 29–30

records.item_title: APGAR vs. Glasgow vs. Ballard vs. Silverman
records.quote: Neonate in distress 0 = no distress · 1–6 = mild-to-moderate · ≥7 = impending respiratory failure The Silverman (Silverman–Andersen) retraction score does not appear anywhere in these 62 decks — look up the Silverman–Andersen retraction score (chest movement, intercostal retraction, xiphoid retraction, nares dilatation, expiratory grunt; each 0–2 ) in a neonatal text.
records.cite: RCP 203 Lssn 2a (Chp 2 – Perform Clinical Assessment), slides 8, 28, 29–30

records.item_title: APGAR vs. Glasgow vs. Ballard vs. Silverman
records.quote: 0 = no distress · 1–6 = mild to moderate distress · ≥7 = impending respiratory failure.
records.cite: RCP 203 Lssn 2a (Chp 2 – Perform Clinical Assessment), slides 8, 28, 29–30

records.item_title: APGAR vs. Glasgow vs. Ballard vs. Silverman
records.quote: Late hypoxemia shows as central cyanosis in room air, or a preductal SpO₂ that will not normalize or falls back below 90% .

records.item_title: L/S Ratio and Mature Surfactant Production
records.quote: Lecithin/sphingomyelin (L/S) ratio > 2:1 indicates fetal lung maturity.
records.cite: Heuer Ch 1 — Maternal and Perinatal/Neonatal History (PDF p53-55) · RCP 203 Lssn 2a notes (explicitly de-emphasised)

records.item_title: L/S Ratio and Mature Surfactant Production
records.quote: Lecithin/albumin (L/A) ratio ≥ 40.0 is the parallel maturity threshold Heuer gives.
records.cite: Heuer Ch 1 — Maternal and Perinatal/Neonatal History (PDF p53-55) · RCP 203 Lssn 2a notes (explicitly de-emphasised)

records.item_title: L/S Ratio and Mature Surfactant Production
records.quote: Surfactant is 85–90% lipid by weight, mostly phosphatidylcholine (75–80%) , plus proteins SP-A, SP-B, SP-C, SP-D .
records.cite: Heuer Ch 1 — Maternal and Perinatal/Neonatal History (PDF p53-55) · RCP 203 Lssn 2a notes (explicitly de-emphasised)

records.item_title: L/S Ratio and Mature Surfactant Production
records.quote: Because 90–95% of surfactant is taken back up by the Type II cell, reprocessed, and re-secreted, one or two doses of exogenous surfactant are usually enough.
records.cite: Heuer Ch 1 — Maternal and Perinatal/Neonatal History (PDF p53-55) · RCP 203 Lssn 2a notes (explicitly de-emphasised)

records.item_title: L/S Ratio and Mature Surfactant Production
records.quote: The basic problem in RDS is lack of surfactant from lung immaturity → high surface tension → higher ventilating pressures needed; prophylaxis is indicated in premature infants < 29 weeks gestational age at high risk, or weighing < 1250 grams at birth.
records.cite: Heuer Ch 1 — Maternal and Perinatal/Neonatal History (PDF p53-55) · RCP 203 Lssn 2a notes (explicitly de-emphasised)

records.item_title: L/S Ratio and Mature Surfactant Production
records.quote: L/S ratio for maturity Explicitly excluded ("do not study… L/S ratio, PG, L/A ratio") Phosphatidylglycerol (PG) Named only in that same exclusion note — no role given Where made / stored Type II alveolar cells ; stored in lamellar bodies ; secretion stimulated by lung inflation Composition Lipids 85–90% by weight; phosphatidylcholine 75–80% ; proteins SP-A, SP-B, SP-C, SP-D Recycling 90–95% reabsorbed and re-secreted → 1–2 doses of exogenous surfactant usually suffice Prematurity thresholds Prophylaxis for RDS at < 29 weeks gestation, or birth weight < 1250 g

records.item_title: Croup vs. Epiglottitis
records.quote: Epiglottitis Both are important causes of upper-airway obstruction in children , and both are dangerous because of pediatric airway anatomy: in children the narrowest point is the cricoid ring , so 1 mm of circumferential edema can cut the airway diameter by more than 50% — the same 1 mm in an adult is merely "noticeable." That is exactly why croup, epiglottitis, post-extubation edema, and airway trauma make pediatric patients deteriorate rapidly.
records.cite: RCP 203 Lssn 2a, slides 60–61; Chptr 6 – Adrenergics, slides 18, 21–22; RCP 105 Wk 1 Lctr 2 – Airway Management, slide 22

records.item_title: Croup vs. Epiglottitis
records.quote: Racemic epinephrine ( 2.25% solution, 0.25–0.5 mL = 5.63–11.25 mg , QID) is the deck's listed treatment for reducing airway swelling in both croup and epiglottitis, as well as post-extubation stridor .
records.cite: RCP 203 Lssn 2a, slides 60–61; Chptr 6 – Adrenergics, slides 18, 21–22; RCP 105 Wk 1 Lctr 2 – Airway Management, slide 22

records.item_title: Croup vs. Epiglottitis
records.quote: Feature Croup (LTB — laryngotracheobronchitis) Epiglottitis Organism Viral — human parainfluenza viruses (HPIV) listed as a cause of croup (infection of larynx, trachea, bronchi) Bacterial — Haemophilus influenzae , which causes invasive disease including epiglottitis ("swelling in the throat") Incubation / onset speed HPIV symptoms appear 2 to 7 days after infection Not stated in the decks (classically abrupt) Age Not stated in the decks ;
records.cite: RCP 203 Lssn 2a, slides 60–61; Chptr 6 – Adrenergics, slides 18, 21–22; RCP 105 Wk 1 Lctr 2 – Airway Management, slide 22

records.item_title: Croup vs. Epiglottitis
records.quote: HPIV affects infants and young children Deck notes epiglottitis has become much less common in children following Hib vaccination Hallmark sign Harsh, barking cough ; stridor with upper-airway obstruction Not stated in the decks — drooling and the tripod position do not appear in any deck Location of swelling Subglottic — narrowing of the airway below the vocal cords from edema/inflammation Supraglottic — swollen epiglottis X-ray sign / view Steeple sign on the AP view Thumb sign on the lateral neck view Treatment named Racemic epinephrine (strong α-adrenergic ) to reduce airway swelling — 2.25% , 0.25–0.5 mL SVN, QID Racemic epinephrine listed for the same purpose; airway management takes priority over the x-ray if unstable Do-not-examine-the-throat rule Not covered in the available slide decks.
records.cite: RCP 203 Lssn 2a, slides 60–61; Chptr 6 – Adrenergics, slides 18, 21–22; RCP 105 Wk 1 Lctr 2 – Airway Management, slide 22

records.item_title: Obstructive (OSA) vs. Central Sleep Apnea (CSA)
records.quote: OSA affects roughly 25% of U.S. adults and is a major cause of excessive daytime sleepiness .
records.cite: Sleep Apnea deck, slides 5–10, 14, 17–22, 25, 34–37

records.item_title: Obstructive (OSA) vs. Central Sleep Apnea (CSA)
records.quote: Feature OSA CSA Mechanism Recurrent collapse of the upper airway ; airflow absent/near-absent but ventilatory effort persists ; genioglossus fails to oppose collapsing forces, tongue falls into oropharynx Airway open , but brain fails to signal — both airflow AND ventilatory effort stop or decrease Classification Cardinal features: obstructive apneas , hypopneas , RERAs ; episodes often end with fricative breathing (snorting) Primary (idiopathic) vs. secondary ; subtypes = hyperventilation-related (most common: primary CSA, Cheyne-Stokes , high altitude) and hypoventilation-related (CNS depressants, neuromuscular disease, severe COPD) Risk factors / causes Obesity (strongest predictor), large neck size , male sex , age > 65 , hypertension, diabetes, chronic nasal congestion, family history, alcohol, sedatives, smoking , ethnicity (higher in Black, Hispanic, Pacific Islander populations under age 35 ) Heart failure with Cheyne-Stokes breathing, CNS/brain stem lesions or injury , drugs (opioids, alcohol, benzodiazepines), high altitude , neuromuscular disease (Guillain-Barré, myasthenia gravis); atrial fibrillation often associated Definitions to know Hypopnea = airflow ↓ ≥ 30% for ≥ 10 sec with ≥ 3% SpO₂ drop or arousal;
records.cite: Sleep Apnea deck, slides 5–10, 14, 17–22, 25, 34–37

records.item_title: Obstructive (OSA) vs. Central Sleep Apnea (CSA)
records.quote: RERA = ↑ effort/flattened nasal pressure ≥ 10 sec ending in arousal, not meeting apnea/hypopnea criteria Majority of events are central apneas/hypopneas Diagnosis Full-night attended in-lab polysomnography (PSG) = gold standard ; split-night = first half diagnostic, second half CPAP/BiPAP titration; home sleep test uses total recording time and reports RDI instead of AHI (no EEG → can't measure total sleep time) PSG showing absent airflow AND absent thoracoabdominal movement ; evaluate for cardiac disease and brain stem/cerebral cortex lesions Diagnostic AHI thresholds Confirmed when AHI ≥ 15/hr in an asymptomatic patient, OR AHI ≥ 5/hr with symptoms (sleepiness, fatigue, snoring, pauses);
records.cite: Sleep Apnea deck, slides 5–10, 14, 17–22, 25, 34–37

records.item_title: Obstructive (OSA) vs. Central Sleep Apnea (CSA)
records.quote: 75% of events must be obstructive.
records.cite: Sleep Apnea deck, slides 5–10, 14, 17–22, 25, 34–37

records.item_title: Obstructive (OSA) vs. Central Sleep Apnea (CSA)
records.quote: AHI = (apneas + hypopneas) ÷ total sleep time in hours (e.g., 100 events ÷ 8 hr = 12.5/hr ) Severity thresholds by AHI are stated for OSA only in the deck Severity Mild 5–15/hr (occasional daytime sleepiness);
records.cite: Sleep Apnea deck, slides 5–10, 14, 17–22, 25, 34–37

records.item_title: Obstructive (OSA) vs. Central Sleep Apnea (CSA)
records.quote: Severe > 30/hr or SpO₂ < 90% for > 20% of sleep time (high accident risk, pulmonary hypertension, arrhythmias, cor pulmonale) — Treatment Behavior modification (weight loss most effective, exercise, avoid alcohol/sedatives, avoid supine position) + PAP = first-line :
records.cite: Sleep Apnea deck, slides 5–10, 14, 17–22, 25, 34–37

records.item_title: Lab Values and Presentation: Bacterial PNA vs. Emphysema vs. PE vs. Pulmonary Fibrosis
records.quote: Condition Presentation CXR ABG pattern Labs Key distinguishing feature Bacterial Pneumonia Diaphoretic, cyanotic , tachypnea ; crackles, bronchial breath sounds, whispered pectoriloquy ; dull percussion; cough starts dry → productive yellow/green, rust-colored sputum or hemoptysis ; fever > 101°F (viral < 101°F ), ↑ HR, ↑ RR, ↑ BP ↑ density from consolidation/atelectasis ; air bronchograms (classic); possible abscess with air-fluid level or pleural effusion/empyema Early: respiratory alkalosis with hypoxemia (hyperventilation).
records.cite: Infectious Pulmonary Disease deck, slides 26–27; COPD deck, slides 12–15; Pulmonary Edema and PVD deck, slides 43–45, 48, 55; ILD deck, slides 39–42, 44–46, 49–50

records.item_title: Lab Values and Presentation: Bacterial PNA vs. Emphysema vs. PE vs. Pulmonary Fibrosis
records.quote: Severe: respiratory acidosis with hypoxemia (acute ventilatory failure) CBC: ↑ WBC (bacterial) vs. ↓/normal WBC (viral); sputum culture & sensitivity to identify organism Air bronchograms + ↑ WBC + fever > 101°F ; hypoxemia is from capillary shunting and is refractory to O₂ therapy Emphysema (Type A COPD, " Pink Puffer ") Thin, cachectic , barrel chest , pursed-lip breathing , heavy accessory muscle use, tachypnea; minimal cough, little/no sputum ; pink skin tone; hyperresonant percussion; decreased breath sounds — quiet chest Hyperlucency , hyperinflation , ↑ A-P diameter , flattened/depressed diaphragms , blebs/bullae Compensated (partial or full) respiratory acidosis with hypoxemia ; during exacerbation, acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis Hct/Hgb normal in mild–moderate , may ↑ in late stages; ↓ Cl⁻ and ↑ Na⁺ only in late stages ; sputum usually normal (minimal) ; α₁-antitrypsin < 15–20% of normal is highly suggestive of AATD emphysema ↓ DLCO (alveolar-capillary membrane destroyed) + obstructive PFT: ↓ FEV₁, ↓ FEV₁/FVC, ↓ FEF₂₅₋₇₅ ; pulmonary HTN/cor pulmonale uncommon (vs. common in chronic bronchitis) Pulmonary Embolism (PE) Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, cough ± hemoptysis , wheezing; tachycardia , arrhythmias, right heart strain , ↑ S₂ , weak pulse, hypotension; anxiety, diaphoresis, syncope, cyanosis; leg swelling (DVT clue) Often normal — its role is to rule out pneumonia/pneumothorax ; may show infiltrates or an elevated hemidiaphragm (nonspecific) Mild–moderate: acute alveolar hyperventilation with hypoxemia (↓ PaCO₂, ↑ pH).
records.cite: Infectious Pulmonary Disease deck, slides 26–27; COPD deck, slides 12–15; Pulmonary Edema and PVD deck, slides 43–45, 48, 55; ILD deck, slides 39–42, 44–46, 49–50

records.item_title: Lab Values and Presentation: Bacterial PNA vs. Emphysema vs. PE vs. Pulmonary Fibrosis
records.quote: Severe hypoxia → lactic acidosis drops pH lower than the PaCO₂ predicts D-dimer : normal rules out PE ; elevated > 500 ng/mL only suggests clot and is not specific .
records.cite: Infectious Pulmonary Disease deck, slides 26–27; COPD deck, slides 12–15; Pulmonary Edema and PVD deck, slides 43–45, 48, 55; ILD deck, slides 39–42, 44–46, 49–50

records.item_title: How Hypoxia Appears in an Infant
records.quote: Cyanosis is a major indicator of hypoxemia — check lips, mucosa, tongue (central) and nail beds/fingertips (peripheral) — but remember it only becomes visible when the blood holds at least 5 g/dL of reduced hemoglobin , so a severely anemic infant can be badly hypoxemic without looking cyanotic .
records.cite: RCP 105 Wk 1 Lctr 2 – Airway Management, slide 22; RCP 103 Clinical Data deck, slides 21, 26; RCP 203 Lssn 2a, slides 10–11, 31; Chptr 1 – Intro to Respiratory Care Pharmacology, slide 5

records.item_title: How Hypoxia Appears in an Infant
records.quote: Sign What it means in an infant Tachypnea Earliest compensation — hypoxemia stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors; stiff/low-compliance lungs force rapid, shallow breathing Retractions Chest wall pulled inward on inspiration; signals significant airway obstruction ; more pronounced in children due to increased chest wall compliance Nasal flaring Increased inspiratory effort — a classic pediatric distress sign "See-saw" breathing Thoracic-abdominal dyssynchrony/paradox — chest moves in on inspiration while abdomen moves out; a sign of abnormally high WOB and of damage to the structures of breathing Cyanosis Visible only at ≥ 5 g/dL reduced Hgb ; central (lips, tongue) = dangerous hypoxemia, peripheral (hands, feet) often poor perfusion Apnea Listed specifically as a possible progression in infants (e.g., RSV/bronchiolitis) — adults do not typically do this Accessory muscle use / grunting Accessory muscle use = increased WOB.
records.cite: RCP 105 Wk 1 Lctr 2 – Airway Management, slide 22; RCP 103 Clinical Data deck, slides 21, 26; RCP 203 Lssn 2a, slides 10–11, 31; Chptr 1 – Intro to Respiratory Care Pharmacology, slide 5

records.item_title: How Hypoxia Appears in an Infant
records.quote: 1 mm of circumferential edema in an adult is noticeable but often tolerated, while 1 mm in an infant reduces airway diameter by more than 50% and causes significant distress.
records.cite: RCP 105 Wk 1 Lctr 2 – Airway Management, slide 22; RCP 103 Clinical Data deck, slides 21, 26; RCP 203 Lssn 2a, slides 10–11, 31; Chptr 1 – Intro to Respiratory Care Pharmacology, slide 5
